    ],
    "text": "   - Institutional vs Retail Sentiment Divergence: $\\text{TopTrader}_{L/S} - \\text{Global}_{L/S}$"
  },
  {
    "file": "RESEARCH_QUESTIONS_AND_ANSWERS.md",

    "categories": [
      "leakage_eval"
    ],
    "text": "3. **Stream 3: Point-in-Time US Macroeconomic Announcements (1,030+ Events):**"

  {
    "file": "RESEARCH_QUESTIONS_AND_ANSWERS.md",

    "text": "   - Macro Surprise Score: $Z = (\\text{Actual} - \\text{Forecast}) / \\sigma_{\\text{historical}}$"

# Learning Journal — BTC Full Review

Audit: 2026-11-09T13:10:24.758688+00:00

## Concepts introduced (not mastery assessed)
- Scientific contribution is distinct from ingredient novelty or journal rank.
- Author claims, metadata identity and reproduced performance have different evidence levels.
- Historical data existence is distinct from point-in-time decision availability.
- Indicator parity requires the exact recursion, smoothing and warm-up, not a similar formula.
- Future-dependent support labels need to mature before a prediction.
- Bar-level aggregate flow cannot identify participants or individual cancellations.
- Exclusive labels and executable policies precede model complexity.
- Forward chronology and complete costs precede profitability conclusions.

## Feedback
Earlier confident guidance overstated validated progress. The correct current state is a promising but unvalidated project with a specification requiring repair. No experiments or large data downloads were authorized or performed by this review.

## Practice
1. Identify the first legal time an H=8 support label can be used.
2. Explain which claims survive if a tree model matches few-shot performance.
3. Explain why a 15m candle containing both barriers is not sufficient to know a trade's outcome.

## Next approved milestone
A corrected minimum dataset/label contract, followed by a bounded data-validation pilot only after approval.

Evidence and full findings: `/home/rarebat/ResearchStudio/audits/btc-20261109T131024Z/REVIEW.md`.

````

# Proposed Research Focus: Few-Shot Adaptation of Order-Flow Models Conditioned on News

## Status and scope

This is a **proposed research framing**, not a verified novelty claim, an approved experiment, a proven trading edge or a Q1 acceptance prediction. It preserves the owner's central idea: apply few-shot learning to order flow and news to investigate shortcomings of trading-bot/ML predictions. The Chandelier Exit is a candidate-event generator, not the proposed scientific novelty; VWAP is optional rather than necessary.

The earlier audit remains applicable: indicator parity, calendar correctness, label exclusivity, point-in-time inputs and execution assumptions need repair before experiments. No source project file outside ResearchStudio is modified by this note.

## 1. Result — a specific issue worth testing

**[Hypothesis]** Order-flow models trained on past market conditions may generalize poorly to later regimes, and the relationship between executed aggressor flow and subsequent price paths may differ across scheduled-news contexts. A few-shot adaptation mechanism could use a limited number of legally available, completed examples to adjust predictions in a later regime.

This is a testable proposed failure mode, not an established fact that all order-flow models fail or that few-shot learning must outperform ordinary retraining.

**Research question:**

> Under a fixed, past-only adaptation budget, does news-conditioned few-shot adaptation improve an executed-order-flow model's predictions in later BTC intraday regimes compared with ordinary training/retraining using the same inputs?

**Potential mechanism to investigate:** select or weight support examples using both executed-flow patterns and the news context known at the decision time. Compare this with generic support selection and ordinary feature concatenation. Do not describe this proposed mechanism as novel until the closest-work search is complete.

## 2. Evidence and boundaries

- Wood, Kessler, Roberts and Zohren (2024), *Few-Shot Learning Patterns in Financial Time Series for Trend-Following Strategies*. DOI: https://doi.org/10.3905/jfds.2024.1.157 ; acquired version https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.10500v2 . Access: `full_text` local preprint, canonical journal metadata separately checked. It motivates few-shot regime/context adaptation; it does not validate our proposed order-flow/news repair mechanism. Author-reported trading performance was not reproduced.
- Zhang et al. (2025), *CAMEF: Causal-Augmented Multi-Modality Event-Driven Financial Forecasting by Integrating Time Series Patterns and Salient Macroeconomic Announcements*. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1145/3711896.3736872 ; https://arxiv.org/html/2502.04592v3 . Access: `full_text` preprint plus verified proceedings metadata. It is related macroeconomic multimodal forecasting, not proof that our particular adaptation method is solved or novel.
- The prior audit records related news-based few-shot work and 15m OI meta-labeling, plus important null/mixed evidence. A dedicated closest-work review of few-shot/domain adaptation with order flow remains necessary.

For the current free BTC kline dataset, **order flow means executed buyer/seller aggressor volume and derived rolling measures**. It does not mean a complete order-level history, institutional identities or validated spoofing detection. Scheduled-news clocks are not pre-release surprise values or breaking-news text. Any broader claim requires matching data.

## 3. Decision — isolate the proposed contribution

A minimum controlled comparison uses four conditions:

1. Ordinary ML with executed order flow.
2. Ordinary ML with executed order flow plus legally available news context.
3. Few-shot adaptation with executed order flow.
4. Few-shot adaptation with executed order flow plus the same news context.

Use the same signal candidates, outcome definitions, train/validation/test dates, information availability, tuning resources and execution assumptions. Add a support-selection ablation comparing news-conditioned selection with a generic selection rule. Compare a regularized linear model and a tree model; the proposed few-shot model family must be selected explicitly rather than conflating X-Trend with a prototypical MLP.

Specify what a task/new regime is, how it is identified online, how many matured labels are permitted, and when support updates occur. Regime/domain adaptation with fixed outcome classes is not automatically the same as few-shot recognition of entirely new classes.

### Outcomes and metrics — proposed, not preregistered

- Define exclusive TP-first/SL-first/timeout outcomes for one executable policy before adding descriptive trajectory archetypes.
- Select one predictive primary metric in the protocol, such as probability log loss over the same candidate events. Report calibration and uncertainty.
- Evaluate fee/funding/spread-adjusted economic results separately under a common risk budget; prediction improvements are not automatically profits.
- Freeze temporal holdouts and the adaptation/tuning budget. All learned transforms and support-selection rules must be fit using legal past information.

## 4. Confidence, uncertainty and falsifiers

**[Agent Inference]** This focused question is a plausible applied-research direction. It is stronger than an ingredient-list contribution only if it establishes a previously inadequately measured adaptation problem and a defensible finding or mechanism.

**[Hypothesis]** Joint news/flow conditioning helps few-shot adaptation beyond the same information in ordinary ML. Profitability, superiority, novelty and publication acceptance are unknown.

Falsifiers include:
- Flow-plus-news ordinary ML matches or beats the few-shot method under the same legal inputs and resources.
- News conditioning adds no repeatable benefit over flow-only few-shot adaptation.
- Apparent improvement vanishes under chronological testing, matured-label support rules or realistic costs.
- The chosen baseline does not suffer the proposed adaptation problem.

A null result must be preserved. It may provide useful knowledge, but a negative result is not automatically a strong publication without a consequential question and rigorous design.

## 5. Next step and approval gate

First document the proposed baseline failure and define the adaptation task and falsifier. Then repair the minimum dataset/label contract before a bounded, owner-approved pilot. No training, packages, large downloads or external contacts are authorized by this note.

Protocol approval: **not yet granted**. Model family, shot budget, holdout dates, primary metric, compute budget and experiment execution remain to be agreed.

## 6. Learning note and exercise

The four-condition comparison separates the value of additional news information from the value of few-shot adaptation. Without ordinary ML plus the same news inputs, an improvement cannot fairly be credited to few-shot learning.

**Exercise:** The joint few-shot model beats an order-flow-only baseline but ties ordinary ML with order flow plus news. What did the comparison establish, and which few-shot superiority claim must be withdrawn?

Concepts introduced: hypothesis versus promised outcome; information-matched baselines; few-shot domain/regime adaptation; label maturity; predictive versus economic value. Owner mastery has not been assessed.

aria-label=\"Copy link to solution\" data-clipboard-text=\"\" class=\"copy-link-button-lx2zmbpH lightButton-kjRfTlfx noContent-kjRfTlfx withStartSlot-kjRfTlfx quiet-primary-IeQwPjcZ gray-IeQwPjcZ class=\"bodyWrapper-Nnq2zDWE\"><div><div itemscope=\"\" itemProp=\"acceptedAnswer\" itemType=\"https://schema.org/Answer\"><div itemProp=\"text\" class=\"solution-Rn_86zzR solution-ZemkGI_Z code-highlighter-lTpRmCvM\"><h4><span class=\"fr-video fr-deletable fr-fvc fr-dvb fr-draggable\"><iframe src=\"https://www.youtube.com/embed/kFx5eL5JtSU??si=6qLc_fxVniUwOIg9&amp;wmode=opaque\" frameborder=\"0\" allowfullscreen=\"\" class=\"fr-draggable\"></iframe></span><br></h4><h4>Definition</h4><p><a href=\"https://www.tradingview.com/scripts/averagetruerange/\" rel=\"noreferrer noopener\">The Average True Range (ATR)</a> is a tool used in technical analysis to measure volatility. Unlike many of today's popular indicators, the ATR is not used to indicate the direction of price. Rather, it is a metric used solely to measure volatility, especially volatility caused by price gaps or limit moves.</p><p><iframe src=\"https://www.tradingview.com/widgetembed/?frameElementId=tradingview_683fc&amp;symbol=GOOGL&amp;interval=D&amp;hidetoptoolbar=1&amp;hidesidetoolbar=1&amp;symboledit=1&amp;saveimage=0&amp;toolbarbg=000000&amp;studies=ATR%40tv-basicstudies&amp;hideideas=1&amp;theme=White&amp;style=1&amp;timezone=Etc%2FUTC&amp;hidevolume=1&amp;padding=0&amp;studies_overrides=%7B%7D&amp;overrides=%7B%7D&amp;enabled_features=%5B%5D&amp;disabled_features=%5B%5D&amp;locale=en&amp;utm_source=www.tradingview.com&amp;utm_medium=widget&amp;utm_campaign=chart&amp;utm_term=GOOGL\" frameborder=\"0\" allowfullscreen=\"\"></iframe></p><p>If you want to screen instruments with the ATR, you can either open the desired screener from the right toolbar in the \"Products\" menu or access the standalone screener from the home page.</p><p><div data-img-border=\"\"><img src=\"https://s3.amazonaws.com/cdn.freshdesk.com/data/helpdesk/attachments/production/43600746588/original/8GFRRyUDxZOKzSkaBrgwGt0Kt6orb1tdUQ.png?1767956064\"></div></p><p>From there, click the \"Add new filter\" button and select the ATR you need — the standard one or the&nbsp;</p><p><a href=\"https://www.tradingview.com/support/solutions/43000734653/\">ATR%</a>.</p><div data-img-border=\"\"><img src=\"https://s3.amazonaws.com/cdn.freshdesk.com/data/helpdesk/attachments/production/43600747102/original/tTDoGNPIEghtBINyaRVQTcNxEZuuFNVmew.png?1767956226\"></div><h4>History</h4><p>J. Welles Wilder created the ATR and featured it in his book <em>New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems</em>. The book was published in 1978 and also featured several of his now classic indicators such as; The Relative Strength Index, Average Directional Index and the Parabolic SAR. Much like the indicators mentioned, the ATR is still widely used and has great importance in the world of technical analysis.</p><h4>Calculation</h4><p>To calculate the ATR, the True Range first needs to be discovered. True Range takes into account the most current period high/low range as well as the previous period close if necessary. There are three calculation which need to be completed and then compared against each other. The True Range is the largest of the following:</p><pre>The Current Period High minus (-) Current Period Low\nThe Absolute Value (abs) of the Current Period High minus (-) The Previous Period Close\nThe Absolute Value (abs) of the Current Period Low minus (-) The Previous Period Close</pre><pre>true range = max[(high - low), abs(high - previous close), abs (low - previous close)]</pre><p dir=\"ltr\">*Absolute Value is used because the ATR does not measure price direction, only volatility. Therefore there should be no negative numbers. *Once you have the True Range, the Average True Range can be plotted. By default on TradingView the ATR is a Relative Moving Average (RMA) of the True Range, but the smoothing type can be changed to SMA, EMA or WMA&nbsp;in the settings.</p><h4>The basics</h4><p>Average True Range is a continuously plotted line usually kept below the main price chart window. The way to interpret the Average True Range is that the higher the ATR value, then the higher the level of volatility.</p><ul><li>The look back period to use for the ATR is at the trader's discretion however 14 days is the most common.</li><li>ATR can be used with varying periods (daily, weekly, intraday etc.) however daily is typically the period used.</li></ul><h4>What to look for</h4><h5>Measuring the Strength of a Move</h5><p>As previously stated Average True Range does not take into account price direction, therefore it is not used as an active indicator to predict future moves. Instead, it is most useful in measuring the strength of a move. For example, if a security's price makes a move or reversal, either Bullish or Bearish, there will usually be an increase in volatility. In that case, the ATR will be on the rise. This can be used as a way to gauge the underlying strength of the move. The more volatility in a large move, the more interest or pressure there is reinforcing that move.</p><p>On the other hand, during periods of sustained sideways movement, volatility is frequently low. This could assist in the discovery of trading ranges.</p><p><iframe src=\"https://www.tradingview.com/embed/KXbGepIC/\" frameborder=\"0\"></iframe></p><h5>Using Absolute Value</h5><p>The fact that ATR is calculated using absolute values of differences in price is something that should not be ignored. This is relevant because it means that securities with higher price values will inherently have higher ATR values. Likewise, securities with lower price values will have lower ATR values. The consequence is that a trader cannot compare the ATR Values of multiple securities. What is considered to be a high ATR Value or a high ATR Range for one security may not be the same for another security. A trader should study and research the relevance of ATR for each security independently when performing chart analysis.</p><h5>Compare the charts below.</h5><p>Apple (AAPL) has a price over $450 and an ATR over 12.</p><p><iframe src=\"https://www.tradingview.com/embed/cndM4m2p/\" frameborder=\"0\"></iframe></p><p>Ford (F) has a price over $17 and an ATR of less than 1.</p><p><iframe src=\"https://www.tradingview.com/embed/wiWXIn00/\" frameborder=\"0\"></iframe></p><h4>Summary</h4><p>ATR is a nice chart analysis tool for keeping an eye on volatility which is a variable that is always important in charting or investing. It is a good option when trying to gauge the overall strength of a move or for discovering a trading range. That being said, it is an indicator which is best used as a compliment to more price direction driven indicators. Once a move has begun, the ATR can add a level of confidence (or lack there of) in that move which can be rather beneficial.</p><h4>Inputs</h4><div data-img-border=\"\"><img src=\"https://s3.amazonaws.com/cdn.freshdesk.com/data/helpdesk/attachments/production/43582439081/original/d8y2A6wN6N4fY7C1ae_SPGp8Fo_KAReIJA.png?1758720061\"></div><h5>Length</h5><p>The time period to be used in calculating the Average True Range. 14 days is the default.</p><h4>Style</h4><div data-img-border=\"\"><img src=\"https://s3.amazonaws.com/cdn.freshdesk.com/data/helpdesk/attachments/production/43582439174/original/nEuC-nGIHJWgPBv-AYozyldSO1YNTiRhvQ.png?1758720078\"></div><h5>ATR</h5><p>Can toggle the visibility of the ATR Line as well as the visibility of a price line showing the actual current value of the ATR Line. Can also select the ATR Line's color, line thickness and visual type (Line is the default).</p><h5>Precision</h5><p>Sets the number of decimal places to be left on the indicator's value before rounding up. The higher this number, the more decimal points will be on the indicator's value.</p><p dir=\"ltr\">Also read:</p><ul><li dir=\"ltr\"><a href=\"https://www.tradingview.com/support/solutions/43000756695-how-to-trade-on-tradingview/\">How to trade on TradingView</a></li><li dir=\"ltr\"><a (ATR)\",\"description\":\"<h4><span class=\\\"fr-video fr-deletable fr-fvc fr-dvb fr-draggable\\\"><iframe src=\\\"https://www.youtube.com/embed/kFx5eL5JtSU??si=6qLc_fxVniUwOIg9&amp;wmode=opaque\\\" frameborder=\\\"0\\\" allowfullscreen=\\\"\\\" class=\\\"fr-draggable\\\"></iframe></span><br></h4><h4>Definition</h4><p><a href=\\\"https://www.tradingview.com/scripts/averagetruerange/\\\" rel=\\\"noreferrer noopener\\\">The Average True Range (ATR)</a> is a tool used in technical analysis to measure volatility. Unlike many of today's popular indicators, the ATR is not used to indicate the direction of price. Rather, it is a metric used solely to measure volatility, especially volatility caused by price gaps or limit moves.</p><p><iframe src=\\\"https://www.tradingview.com/widgetembed/?frameElementId=tradingview_683fc&amp;symbol=GOOGL&amp;interval=D&amp;hidetoptoolbar=1&amp;hidesidetoolbar=1&amp;symboledit=1&amp;saveimage=0&amp;toolbarbg=000000&amp;studies=ATR%40tv-basicstudies&amp;hideideas=1&amp;theme=White&amp;style=1&amp;timezone=Etc%2FUTC&amp;hidevolume=1&amp;padding=0&amp;studies_overrides=%7B%7D&amp;overrides=%7B%7D&amp;enabled_features=%5B%5D&amp;disabled_features=%5B%5D&amp;locale=en&amp;utm_source=www.tradingview.com&amp;utm_medium=widget&amp;utm_campaign=chart&amp;utm_term=GOOGL\\\" frameborder=\\\"0\\\" allowfullscreen=\\\"\\\"></iframe></p><p>If you want to screen instruments with the ATR, you can either open the desired screener from the right toolbar in the \\\"Products\\\" menu or access the standalone screener from the home page.</p><p><div data-img-border=\\\"\\\"><img src=\\\"https://s3.amazonaws.com/cdn.freshdesk.com/data/helpdesk/attachments/production/43600746588/original/8GFRRyUDxZOKzSkaBrgwGt0Kt6orb1tdUQ.png?1767956064\\\"></div></p><p>From there, click the \\\"Add new filter\\\" button and select the ATR you need — the standard one or the&nbsp;</p><p><a href=\\\"https://www.tradingview.com/support/solutions/43000734653/\\\">ATR%</a>.</p><div data-img-border=\\\"\\\"><img src=\\\"https://s3.amazonaws.com/cdn.freshdesk.com/data/helpdesk/attachments/production/43600747102/original/tTDoGNPIEghtBINyaRVQTcNxEZuuFNVmew.png?1767956226\\\"></div><h4>History</h4><p>J. Welles Wilder created the ATR and featured it in his book <em>New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems</em>. The book was published in 1978 and also featured several of his now classic indicators such as; The Relative Strength Index, Average Directional Index and the Parabolic SAR. Much like the indicators mentioned, the ATR is still widely used and has great importance in the world of technical analysis.</p><h4>Calculation</h4><p>To calculate the ATR, the True Range first needs to be discovered. True Range takes into account the most current period high/low range as well as the previous period close if necessary. There are three calculation which need to be completed and then compared against each other. The True Range is the largest of the following:</p><pre>The Current Period High minus (-) Current Period Low\\nThe Absolute Value (abs) of the Current Period High minus (-) The Previous Period Close\\nThe Absolute Value (abs) of the Current Period Low minus (-) The Previous Period Close</pre><pre>true range = max[(high - low), abs(high - previous close), abs (low - previous close)]</pre><p dir=\\\"ltr\\\">*Absolute Value is used because the ATR does not measure price direction, only volatility. Therefore there should be no negative numbers. *Once you have the True Range, the Average True Range can be plotted. By default on TradingView the ATR is a Relative Moving Average (RMA) of the True Range, but the smoothing type can be changed to SMA, EMA or WMA&nbsp;in the settings.</p><h4>The basics</h4><p>Average True Range is a continuously plotted line usually kept below the main price chart window. The way to interpret the Average True Range is that the higher the ATR value, then the higher the level of volatility.</p><ul><li>The look back period to use for the ATR is at the trader's discretion however 14 days is the most common.</li><li>ATR can be used with varying periods (daily, weekly, intraday etc.) however daily is typically the period used.</li></ul><h4>What to look for</h4><h5>Measuring the Strength of a Move</h5><p>As previously stated Average True Range does not take into account price direction, therefore it is not used as an active indicator to predict future moves. Instead, it is most useful in measuring the strength of a move. For example, if a security's price makes a move or reversal, either Bullish or Bearish, there will usually be an increase in volatility. In that case, the ATR will be on the rise. This can be used as a way to gauge the underlying strength of the move. The more volatility in a large move, the more interest or pressure there is reinforcing that move.</p><p>On the other hand, during periods of sustained sideways movement, volatility is frequently low. This could assist in the discovery of trading ranges.</p><p><iframe src=\\\"https://www.tradingview.com/embed/KXbGepIC/\\\" frameborder=\\\"0\\\"></iframe></p><h5>Using Absolute Value</h5><p>The fact that ATR is calculated using absolute values of differences in price is something that should not be ignored. This is relevant because it means that securities with higher price values will inherently have higher ATR values. Likewise, securities with lower price values will have lower ATR values. The consequence is that a trader cannot compare the ATR Values of multiple securities. What is considered to be a high ATR Value or a high ATR Range for one security may not be the same for another security. A trader should study and research the relevance of ATR for each security independently when performing chart analysis.</p><h5>Compare the charts below.</h5><p>Apple (AAPL) has a price over $450 and an ATR over 12.</p><p><iframe src=\\\"https://www.tradingview.com/embed/cndM4m2p/\\\" frameborder=\\\"0\\\"></iframe></p><p>Ford (F) has a price over $17 and an ATR of less than 1.</p><p><iframe src=\\\"https://www.tradingview.com/embed/wiWXIn00/\\\" frameborder=\\\"0\\\"></iframe></p><h4>Summary</h4><p>ATR is a nice chart analysis tool for keeping an eye on volatility which is a variable that is always important in charting or investing. It is a good option when trying to gauge the overall strength of a move or for discovering a trading range. That being said, it is an indicator which is best used as a compliment to more price direction driven indicators. Once a move has begun, the ATR can add a level of confidence (or lack there of) in that move which can be rather beneficial.</p><h4>Inputs</h4><div data-img-border=\\\"\\\"><img src=\\\"https://s3.amazonaws.com/cdn.freshdesk.com/data/helpdesk/attachments/production/43582439081/original/d8y2A6wN6N4fY7C1ae_SPGp8Fo_KAReIJA.png?1758720061\\\"></div><h5>Length</h5><p>The time period to be used in calculating the Average True Range. 14 days is the default.</p><h4>Style</h4><div data-img-border=\\\"\\\"><img src=\\\"https://s3.amazonaws.com/cdn.freshdesk.com/data/helpdesk/attachments/production/43582439174/original/nEuC-nGIHJWgPBv-AYozyldSO1YNTiRhvQ.png?1758720078\\\"></div><h5>ATR</h5><p>Can toggle the visibility of the ATR Line as well as the visibility of a price line showing the actual current value of the ATR Line. Can also select the ATR Line's color, line thickness and visual type (Line is the default).</p><h5>Precision</h5><p>Sets the number of decimal places to be left on the indicator's value before rounding up. The higher this number, the more decimal points will be on the indicator's value.</p><p dir=\\\"ltr\\\">Also read:</p><ul><li dir=\\\"ltr\\\"><a href=\\\"https://www.tradingview.com/support/solutions/43000756695-how-to-trade-on-tradingview/\\\">How to trade on TradingView</a></li><li dir=\\\"ltr\\\"><a       "text": "Average True Range (ATR) — TradingView\n Search\n Products\n Community\n Markets\n Brokers\n More\n EN\nGet started\nHelp Center\n/Knowledge base\n/\nIndicators\n/Built-in Indicators\n/Average True Range (ATR)\nAverage True Range (ATR)\nDefinition\nThe Average True Range (ATR) is a tool used in technical analysis to measure volatility. Unlike many of today's popular indicators, the ATR is not used to indicate the direction of price. Rather, it is a metric used solely to measure volatility, especially volatility caused by price gaps or limit moves.\nIf you want to screen instruments with the ATR, you can either open the desired screener from the right toolbar in the \"Products\" menu or access the standalone screener from the home page.\nFrom there, click the \"Add new filter\" button and select the ATR you need — the standard one or the \nATR%.\nHistory\nJ. Welles Wilder created the ATR and featured it in his book New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems. The book was published in 1978 and also featured several of his now classic indicators such as; The Relative Strength Index, Average Directional Index and the Parabolic SAR. Much like the indicators mentioned, the ATR is still widely used and has great importance in the world of technical analysis.\nCalculation\nTo calculate the ATR, the True Range first needs to be discovered. True Range takes into account the most current period high/low range as well as the previous period close if necessary. There are three calculation which need to be completed and then compared against each other. The True Range is the largest of the following:The Current Period High minus (-) Current Period Low\nThe Absolute Value (abs) of the Current Period High minus (-) The Previous Period Close\nThe Absolute Value (abs) of the Current Period Low minus (-) The Previous Period Closetrue range = max[(high - low), abs(high - previous close), abs (low - previous close)]\n*Absolute Value is used because the ATR does not measure price direction, only volatility. Therefore there should be no negative numbers. *Once you have the True Range, the Average True Range can be plotted. By default on TradingView the ATR is a Relative Moving Average (RMA) of the True Range, but the smoothing type can be changed to SMA, EMA or WMA in the settings.\nThe basics\nAverage True Range is a continuously plotted line usually kept below the main price chart window. The way to interpret the Average True Range is that the higher the ATR value, then the higher the level of volatility.\nThe look back period to use for the ATR is at the trader's discretion however 14 days is the most common.\nATR can be used with varying periods (daily, weekly, intraday etc.) however daily is typically the period used.\nWhat to look forMeasuring the Strength of a Move\nAs previously stated Average True Range does not take into account price direction, therefore it is not used as an active indicator to predict future moves. Instead, it is most useful in measuring the strength of a move. For example, if a security's price makes a move or reversal, either Bullish or Bearish, there will usually be an increase in volatility. In that case, the ATR will be on the rise. This can be used as a way to gauge the underlying strength of the move. The more volatility in a large move, the more interest or pressure there is reinforcing that move.\nOn the other hand, during periods of sustained sideways movement, volatility is frequently low. This could assist in the discovery of trading ranges.\nUsing Absolute Value\nThe fact that ATR is calculated using absolute values of differences in price is something that should not be ignored. This is relevant because it means that securities with higher price values will inherently have higher ATR values. Likewise, securities with lower price values will have lower ATR values. The consequence is that a trader cannot compare the ATR Values of multiple securities. What is considered to be a high ATR Value or a high ATR Range for one security may not be the same for another security. A trader should study and research the relevance of ATR for each security independently when performing chart analysis.Compare the charts below.\nApple (AAPL) has a price over $450 and an ATR over 12.\nFord (F) has a price over $17 and an ATR of less than 1.\nSummary\nATR is a nice chart analysis tool for keeping an eye on volatility which is a variable that is always important in charting or investing. It is a good option when trying to gauge the overall strength of a move or for discovering a trading range. That being said, it is an indicator which is best used as a compliment to more price direction driven indicators. Once a move has begun, the ATR can add a level of confidence (or lack there of) in that move which can be rather beneficial.\nInputs\nLength\nThe time period to be used in calculating the Average True Range. 14 days is the default.\nStyle\nATR\nCan toggle the visibility of the ATR Line as well as the visibility of a price line showing the actual current value of the ATR Line. Can also select the ATR Line's color, line thickness and visual type (Line is the default).Precision\nSets the number of decimal places to be left on the indicator's value before rounding up. The higher this number, the more decimal points will be on the indicator's value.\nAlso read:\nHow to trade on TradingView\nPaper Trading — main functionality\nThe technical analysis essentials\nIntroduction to fundamental analysis\nPortfolios: track your assets, know your trades\nPrevious\nAverage transaction volume\nNext\nAwesome Oscillator (AO)\nLaunch Supercharts\nMade by humans\nEnglish\nSelect market data provided by ICE Data Services. The marker draws no box. */\n  .arxiv-html-header { display: contents; }\n  html[data-reading-mode=\"enabled\"] :is(.arxiv-html-site-chrome, .arxiv-html-header, .ds-site-footer) { display: none; }\n  /* The paper controls' icons are blocks, so they sit centred (the pinned JS shows the theme\n     icon by making its span a block). */\n  .arxiv-html-site-chrome .ds-site-header-tools svg { display: block; width: 18px; height: 18px; flex-shrink: 0; fill: currentColor; }\n  /* ar5iv dims every image in dark mode and puts it on a white wash, for paper figures;\n     arXiv's own render as they are (the logo on the bar, the funder logos on their white\n     chips). Important: ar5iv's dark rules are unlayered, as specific as\n     :root:not([data-theme]) img:not(.ltx_no_dark_filter). */\n  :is(.ds-site-header, .ds-site-footer) img { filter: none !important; }\n  .ds-site-header img { background-color: transparent !important; }\n\n  /* Wide (the theme's 1280px): the theme lays the body out as a grid whose full-width top rows\n     were the band's and its sticky reader bar's. The band takes the first and scrolls away; the\n     header, the paper's bar (no site navigation, the paper's controls), takes the second and\n     stays in view, the one sticky bar, with the anchor clearance that requires (DESIGN-POLICIES).\n     The controls show their names. */\n  @media (min-width: 1280px) {\n    html { scroll-padding-top: 80px; }\n    .arxiv-html-site-chrome { display: contents; }\n    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > #ds-announcement { grid-area: announce; }\n    .arxiv-html-site-chrome > .ds-site-header { grid-area: header; position: sticky; top: 0; z-index: 3; }\n    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-icon { display: none; }\n  }\n  /* Narrow: the header scrolls away, and the controls show icons (names kept for screen\n     readers; Why HTML? goes). The theme's contents panel is fixed below where its old sticky\n     bar was, and hidden only once the reader has closed it, so until then it is an invisible box\n     over the header and the paper: it shows only while open, under the chrome, in its place in\n     the page. The paper's footer (build logs, reporting instructions) keeps the text's side\n     inset; the theme gives it none, so it met the screen edges. */\n  @media (max-width: 1279px) {\n    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-wide { display: none; }\n    .arxiv-html-site-chrome .tool-label { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; }\n    html:not([data-toc-display=\"block\"]) .ltx_page_navbar { display: none; }\n    .ltx_page_navbar { position: absolute; top: auto; }\n    .arxiv-html-footer { padding-inline: 1rem; }\n  }\n</style></head>\n<body>\n<a href=\"#infobox\" class=\"ds-skip-link\">Skip to main content</a>\n<dialog id=\"modal-form\" aria-labelledby=\"modal-title\" closedby=\"any\">\n  <form id=\"modal-form-content\" method=\"dialog\" enctype=\"multipart/form-data\">\n    <header class=\"modal-header\">\n      <h5 id=\"modal-title\" class=\"modal-title\">Report GitHub Issue</h5>\n      <button type=\"submit\" formnovalidate class=\"modal-close\" aria-label=\"Close\">×</button>\n    </header>\n\n    <div class=\"modal-body\">\n      <label for=\"form_title\">Title:</label>\n      <input class=\"form-control\" id=\"form_title\" name=\"form_title\" required placeholder=\"Enter title\">\n\n      <p id=\"selectedTextModalDescription\" hidden>Content selection saved. id=\"abstract1\" class=\"ltx_abstract\"><h6 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_abstract\">Abstract.</h6>\n    \n<p id=\"abstract1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Accurately forecasting the impact of macroeconomic events is critical for investors and policymakers. Salient events like monetary policy decisions and employment reports often trigger market movements by shaping expectations of economic growth and risk, thereby establishing causal relationships between events and market behavior. Existing forecasting methods typically focus either on textual analysis or time-series modeling, but fail to capture the multi-modal nature of financial markets and the causal relationship between events and price movements. To address these gaps, we propose <span id=\"abstract1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">CAMEF</span> (Causal-Augmented Multi-Modality Event-Driven Financial Forecasting), a multi-modality framework that effectively integrates textual and time-series data with a causal learning mechanism and an LLM-based counterfactual event augmentation technique for causal-enhanced financial forecasting. Our contributions include: (1) a multi-modal framework that captures causal relationships between policy texts and historical price data; (2) a new financial dataset with six types of macroeconomic releases from 2008 to April 2024, and high-frequency real trading data for five key U.S. financial assets; and (3) an LLM-based counterfactual event augmentation strategy. We compare CAMEF to state-of-the-art transformer-based time-series and multi-modal baselines, and perform ablation studies to validate the effectiveness of the causal learning mechanism and event types.</p>\n  \n</div>\n<div class=\"ltx_keywords\">\n<h6 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_keywords\">Keywords: </h6>Multimodal learning, Causal Learning, Financial dataset, Time-series Forecasting\n</div>\n<section id=\"S1\" class=\"ltx_section\">\n<h2 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_section\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_section\">1. </span>Introduction</h2>\n\n<div id=\"S1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The prices of financial assets reflect all available information, according to Fama’s Efficient Market Theory <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib16\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Fama, 1965</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib17\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Fama et al., 1969</a>)</cite>. Major financial releases from government sectors often trigger market movements by shaping investors’ expectations and evaluations of economic conditions, asset growth potential, and associated risks. For example, during the FOMC meeting on March 16, 2020, the Fed’s emergency rate cut to 0-0.25% sharply altered investors’ economic outlook, resulting in a massive sell-off. Major indices, including the S&amp;P 500, NASDAQ, and Dow Jones, dropped by over 10%, marking the steepest single-day decline since 1987 <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib14\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Domm, 2021</a>)</cite>. These salient macroeconomic events cause reactions in financial assets, establishing causal relationships between events and financial assets. Figure <a href=\"#S1.F1\" title=\"Figure 1 ‣ 1. Introduction ‣ CAMEF: Causal-Augmented Multi-Modality Event-Driven Financial Forecasting by Integrating Time Series Patterns and Salient Macroeconomic Announcements\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">1</span></a> illustrates multiple types of events that cause financial market reactions. Therefore, <span id=\"S1.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">accurately forecasting the causal consequences of the salient macroeconomic releases on financial market is essential, not only to help investors manage risks and maximize returns, but also to provide policymakers with valuable insights for evaluating and refining future policies.</span></p>\n</div>\n<figure id=\"S1.F1\" class=\"ltx_figure\"><img src=\"2502.04592v3/figures/multi-model-demo.drawio.png\" id=\"S1.F1.g1\" class=\"ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape\" style=\"aspect-ratio:381/189;\" width=\"381\" height=\"189\" alt=\"Refer to caption\">\n<figcaption class=\"ltx_caption ltx_centering\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure\"><span id=\"S1.F1.3\" class=\"ltx_text\" style=\"font-size:90%;\">Figure 1</span>. </span><span id=\"S1.F1.4\" class=\"ltx_text\" style=\"font-size:90%;\">Event-Driven Forecasting Examples: (a) Market reaction to employment insurance release; (b) Market reaction during FOMC meeting; (c) Forecasting market reactions to future events.</span></figcaption>\n</figure>\n<div id=\"S1.p2\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S1.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Previous studies on event-driven forecasting have primarily adopted three lines of methodologies. The first line of approaches utilizes text feature-based models, where language models, ranging from self-crafted RNN-based architectures <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib23\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Huynh et al., 2017</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib30\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Liu, 2018</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib12\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Daigo Tashiro and Sakaji, 2019</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib58\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Xu and Cohen, 2018</a>)</cite> to pre-trained transformers <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib63\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Zhou et al., [n. d.]</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib50\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Shah et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, embed sentiment information into text vectors, and then stock movements are predicted as a binary classification task (e.g., hawkish vs. dovish). The second line of methodology focuses on historical time-series data, treating stock price movements as a regression problem <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib55\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Taylor, 2007</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib8\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Cao and Tsay, 1992</a>)</cite>. Recently, transformer-based architectures have been applied for time-series prediction, including Informer <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib61\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Zhou et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, FedFormer <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib62\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Zhou et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, and AutoFormer <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib9\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Chen et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, etc. However, both of these directions typically focus on a single modality, neglecting multi-dimensional information. The third line of research adopts a multi-modality approach, leveraging multiple types of data sources to enhance forecasting performance. For instance, studies like <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib36\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Mathur et al., 2022</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib38\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Ouyang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> incorporate textual, video, and audio data from FOMC meetings alongside corresponding market movements. While these approaches show promise for event-driven financial forecasts, they face three major limitations:</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S1.p3\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<ul id=\"S1.I1\" class=\"ltx_itemize\">\n<li id=\"S1.I1.i1\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"S1.I1.i1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S1.I1.i1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Data Limitation:</span> Existing approaches predominantly focus on a single type of event, such as FOMC meetings <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib50\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Shah et al., 2023</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib36\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Mathur et al., 2022</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib38\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Ouyang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, while neglecting other crucial macroeconomic events like unemployment insurance releases, CPI, PPI, and GDP advance reports. Additionally, many studies rely on daily-based time-series data for financial assets <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib50\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Shah et al., 2023</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib36\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Mathur et al., 2022</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib38\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Ouyang et al., 2024</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib55\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Taylor, 2007</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib8\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Cao and Tsay, 1992</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib61\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Zhou et al., 2021</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib62\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Zhou et al., 2022</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib9\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Chen et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, which limits their applicability and precision in real-time trading scenarios where high-frequency data is mostly adopted.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"S1.I1.i2\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"S1.I1.i2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S1.I1.i2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Modality Limitation:</span> Most prior studies rely on single-modality analysis, using either textual models <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib23\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Huynh et al., 2017</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib30\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Liu, 2018</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib12\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Daigo Tashiro and Sakaji, 2019</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib58\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Xu and Cohen, 2018</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib63\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Zhou et al., [n. d.]</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib50\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Shah et al., 2023</a>)</cite> or time-series models <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib55\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Taylor, 2007</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib8\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Cao and Tsay, 1992</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib61\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Zhou et al., 2021</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib62\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Zhou et al., 2022</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib9\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Chen et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, which fail to integrate the complementary strengths of both modalities. While some multi-modality approaches have been proposed <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib36\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Mathur et al., 2022</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib38\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Ouyang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, they often lack advanced mechanisms for feature fusion, effective decoding strategies, and causal learning, which are critical for understanding the complex interplay between event texts and market dynamics.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"S1.I1.i3\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"S1.I1.i3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S1.I1.i3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Causality Limitation:</span> Existing methods <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib36\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Mathur et al., 2022</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib38\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Ouyang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> fail to incorporate causal reasoning frameworks, overlooking the causal relationships between events and market reactions. Without explicitly modeling these relationships, such approaches cannot fully capture the drivers of financial market behavior, limiting their predictive robustness.</p>\n</div></li>\n</ul>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S1.p4\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S1.p4.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">To address the limitations of previous studies, we propose a novel multi-modality framework, <span id=\"S1.p4.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">CAMEF<span id=\"footnote1\" class=\"ltx_note ltx_role_footnote\"><sup class=\"ltx_note_mark\">1</sup><span class=\"ltx_note_outer\"><span class=\"ltx_note_content\"><sup class=\"ltx_note_mark\">1</sup>\n              <span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_note\"><span id=\"footnote1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_medium\">1</span></span>\n              \n              \n              \n            <span id=\"footnote1.6\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_medium ltx_font_italic\">The dataset and code for CAMEF are open-sourced at: https://github.com/lakebodhi/CAMEF</span></span></span></span></span> (<span id=\"S1.p4.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">c</span>ausal-<span id=\"S1.p4.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">A</span>ugmented <span id=\"S1.p4.1.4\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">M</span>ulti-Modality <span id=\"S1.p4.1.5\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">E</span>vent-Driven Financial <span id=\"S1.p4.1.6\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">F</span>orecasting). CAMEF integrates time-series and textual features through specially designed multi-feature fusion techniques, time-series decoding mechanisms, and causal learning strategies. By conducting a thorough review of financial literature, we identify six types of salient macroeconomic events for the forecasting analysis. Furthermore, the framework employs causal data augmentation powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) and a causal contrastive learning approach to enhance the causal understanding and forecast accuracy of CAMEF. This paper offers three key contributions:</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S1.p5\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<ul id=\"S1.I2\" class=\"ltx_itemize\">\n<li id=\"S1.I2.i1\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"S1.I2.i1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S1.I2.i1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S1.I2.i1.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Novel Dataset:</span> We introduce a novel open-source synthetic dataset comprising 6 types of macroeconomic event scripts (ref to Tab. <a href=\"#S2.T1\" title=\"Table 1 ‣ 2.3. Counterfactual Data Augmentation by LLMs ‣ 2. Related Work ‣ CAMEF: Causal-Augmented Multi-Modality Event-Driven Financial Forecasting by Integrating Time Series Patterns and Salient Macroeconomic Announcements\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">1</span></a> for details) from 2008 to April 2024 through reviewing from financial literature <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib11\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">CIESLAK et al., 2019</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib18\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Gertler and Horvath, 2018</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib35\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Masciandaro et al., 2024</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib45\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Rosa, 2016</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib53\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Tadle, 2022</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib44\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Rosa, 2013</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib34\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">LUCCA and MOENCH, 2015</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib43\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Rosa, 2011</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib39\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Pearce and Roley, 1984</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib19\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Gilbert et al., 2010</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib20\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Gilbert et al., 2017</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib4\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Bartolini et al., 2008</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib27\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Kim et al., 2004</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib21\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Goldberg and Grisse, 2013</a>)</cite>, alongside intra-day _high-frequency financial data at 5-minute intervals from key U.S. stock indexes and Treasury bonds. To support causal learning, the dataset also includes counterfactual event scripts generated using our LLM-based causal argumentation prompting, making it the first to integrate policy texts, high-frequency trading data, and causally augmented content.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"S1.I2.i2\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"S1.I2.i2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S1.I2.i2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S1.I2.i2.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Novel Multi-Modality Model:</span> We propose a novel multi-modality approach, CAMEF, that integrates time-series and textual features, incorporating specifically designed multi-feature fusion and time-series decoding networks, which have been demonstrated to be effective for forecasting. Additionally, the model includes a causal learning mechanism to enhance forecasting capability by capturing the causal relationships between events and market reactions.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"S1.I2.i3\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"S1.I2.i3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S1.I2.i3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S1.I2.i3.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Counterfactual Generation and Learning:</span> We introduce a counterfactual data augmentation strategy to generate counterfactual event scripts based on collected macroeconomic releases. This approach leverages LLMs to create scripts with varying sentiment levels by modifying key numerical values and sentiment-relevant phrases, while preserving the original format, writing style, and neutral words of the factual reports. Counterfactual events enable CAMEF to better understand the causal relationships between events and market reactions by learning from hypothetical scenarios, thereby improving its forecasting ability.</p>\n</div></li>\n</ul>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2\" class=\"ltx_section\">\n<h2 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_section\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_section\">2. </span>Related Work</h2>\n\n<section id=\"S2.SS1\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">2.1. </span>Event-Drive Financial Forecasting</h3>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Event-driven financial forecasting <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib3\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Bao et al., 2025</a>)</cite> focuses on predicting asset prices <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib21\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Goldberg and Grisse, 2013</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib19\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Gilbert et al., 2010</a>)</cite> and market volatility <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib34\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">LUCCA and MOENCH, 2015</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib11\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">CIESLAK et al., 2019</a>)</cite> based on events like macroeconomic releases <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib19\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Gilbert et al., 2010</a>)</cite>, news <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib30\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Liu, 2018</a>)</cite>, corporate announcements <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib63\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Zhou et al., [n. d.]</a>)</cite>, and social media activity <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib58\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Xu and Cohen, 2018</a>)</cite>. Three main approaches exist in this area. The first leverages text analysis to predict asset responses based on event-related text. Early works utilized TF-IDF <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib40\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Pui Cheong Fung et al., 2003</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib29\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Li et al., 2014</a>)</cite> and topic models <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib51\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Si et al., 2013</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib37\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Nguyen et al., 2015</a>)</cite>, progressing to RNN-based models <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib23\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Huynh et al., 2017</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib30\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Liu, 2018</a>)</cite> and pre-trained transformers <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib63\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Zhou et al., [n. d.]</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib50\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Shah et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, which capture nuanced semantics. Although these models excel at semantic extraction, they often lack integration with historical price data, crucial for holistic forecasting.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS1.p2\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS1.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The second line of approaches uses statistical and sequential models on numerical data, such as linear regression <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib6\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Bhuriya et al., 2017</a>)</cite>, ARIMA <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib2\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Ariyo et al., [n. d.]</a>)</cite>, and GARCH <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib24\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Hyup Roh, 2007</a>)</cite>. Later, deep learning methods like RNNs <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib30\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Liu, 2018</a>)</cite> and CNNs <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib49\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Selvin et al., 2017</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib15\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Durairaj and Mohan, 2022</a>)</cite> enhanced nonlinear modeling capabilities. More recently, transformer-based models, such as Informer <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib61\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Zhou et al., 2021</a>)</cite> and FedFormer <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib62\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Zhou et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, improved long-range dependency modeling for time series data. However, these models tend to be “case-specific,” requiring task-specific training. In contrast, the lastest pre-trained models for time-series data, like MOMENT <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib22\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Goswami et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, Timer <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib33\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Liu et al., 2024b</a>)</cite>, and TOKEN <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib54\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Talukder et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, offer more generalized and adaptable solutions for time-series tasks.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS1.p3\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS1.p3.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The third line of research adopts multi-modality approaches, combining diverse data types to improve forecasting accuracy. Some studies incorporate text and audio <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib41\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Qin and Yang, 2019</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib59\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Yang et al., 2020</a>)</cite> but often overlook time-series dependencies. Recent work has integrated time-series and textual data; for example, <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib48\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Sawhney et al., 2020b</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib47\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Sawhney et al., 2020a</a>)</cite> employed SVM and GRU models to capture time-series features. However, these models are relatively shallow for extracting complex patterns. More recent studies <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib28\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Lee et al., 2024</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib25\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Jia et al., 2024</a>)</cite> leverage transformer-based models for time-series analysis, better capturing deeper temporal structures. Building on these advancements, this paper aims to utilize state-of-the-art pre-trained models with enhanced feature fusion and causal learning for multi-modality forecasting.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS2\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">2.2. </span>Salient Macroeconomic Factors</h3>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S2.SS2.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Which macroeconomic announcements have a greater impact on financial markets than others?</span> This question has been widely studied in the financial literature, with Central Bank Communications standing out as the most-researched factor <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib11\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">CIESLAK et al., 2019</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib18\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Gertler and Horvath, 2018</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib35\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Masciandaro et al., 2024</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib45\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Rosa, 2016</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib53\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Tadle, 2022</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib44\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Rosa, 2013</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib34\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">LUCCA and MOENCH, 2015</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib43\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Rosa, 2011</a>)</cite>. Beyond central bank communications, various other macroeconomic factors have also been identified as significant drivers of market movements. Among these, Non-farm Payrolls, Unemployment Releases, Initial Unemployment Claims, ISM Manufacturing Index, GDP Advance Releases, Consumer Confidence Index, and Producer Price Index (PPI) Reports have been found to notably influence price movements and market volatility through empirical statistical testings <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib39\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Pearce and Roley, 1984</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib19\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Gilbert et al., 2010</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib20\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Gilbert et al., 2017</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib4\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Bartolini et al., 2008</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib27\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Kim et al., 2004</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib21\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Goldberg and Grisse, 2013</a>)</cite>. In this paper, we aim to leaverage the most significant factors evidented by the past financial literautre <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib39\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Pearce and Roley, 1984</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib19\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Gilbert et al., 2010</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib20\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Gilbert et al., 2017</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib4\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Bartolini et al., 2008</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib27\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Kim et al., 2004</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib21\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Goldberg and Grisse, 2013</a>)</cite>, which include FOMC Meeting Documents, Non-farm Payrolls, Unemployment Releases, Initial Unemployment Claims, ISM Manufacturing Index, GDP Advance Releases, Consumer Confidence Index, and Producer Price Index (PPI) Reports.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S2.SS3\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">2.3. </span>Counterfactual Data Augmentation by LLMs</h3>\n\n<div id=\"S2.SS3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Counterfactual Data Augmentation seeks to reduce spurious correlations and enhance model robustness. <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet\"><a href=\"#bib.bib26\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Kaushik et al. (2020)</a></cite> introduced a method that augments training data with counterfactuals written by human annotators, effectively helping to mitigate spurious patterns. <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet\"><a href=\"#bib.bib57\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Wu et al. (2021)</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib46\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Ross et al. (2022)</a></cite> later proposed the use of hand-crafted templates and trained text generators to create counterfactual data through predefined perturbation types. However, these methods are limited by their reliance on fixed perturbations. More recently, <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet\"><a href=\"#bib.bib10\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Chen et al. (2023)</a>; <a href=\"#bib.bib56\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Wang et al. (2023)</a></cite> proposed more flexible, LLM-based approaches that leverage specifically designed in-context learning prompts and generation pipelines for counterfactual and instruction data generation. Following this direction, we present a counterfactual generation framework specifically designed for macroeconomic releases.</p>\n</div>\n<figure id=\"S2.T1\" class=\"ltx_table\">\n<figcaption class=\"ltx_caption\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_table\"><span id=\"S2.T1.3\" class=\"ltx_text\" style=\"font-size:90%;\">Table 1</span>. </span><span id=\"S2.T1.4\" class=\"ltx_text\" style=\"font-size:90%;\">Summary of Macroeconomic and Time-Series Data Types, Characteristics and Sources</span></figcaption>\n<table id=\"S2.T1.5\" class=\"ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle\">\n<tr id=\"S2.T1.5.1\" class=\"ltx_tr\">\n<td id=\"S2.T1.5.1.1\" class=\"ltx_td ltx_align_center\">\n<div id=\"S2.T1.5.1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_block ltx_minipage ltx_align_middle\" style=\"width:345.0pt;\">\n<figcaption class=\"ltx_caption ltx_centering\">A. Macroeconomic Event Summary</figcaption>\n<div id=\"S2.T1.5.1.1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer\"
