class=\"ltx_mathvariant_bold\">CAMEF</mtext><mtext>Textual</mtext></msub><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">{</mo><msup><mi id=\"S5.SS5.SSS2.p3.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\mathbf{P}^{GT}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐏</mi><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo lspace=\"0em\" id=\"S5.SS5.SSS2.p3.m2\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\{\\mathbf{P}^{CF}_{i}\\}_{i=1}^{|\\mathbb{E}^{CF}|}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo id=\"S5.SS5.SSS2.p4\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S5.SS5.SSS2.p4.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The time-series encoder is used to encode the historical time-series segment <math id=\"S5.SS5.SSS2.p4.m1\" encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathcal{X}</annotation></semantics></math> aligned with the ground-truth event, resulting in the time-series embedding:</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S5.SS5.SSS2.p5\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<table id=\"S5.E16\" class=\"ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table\">\n\n<tbody><tr class=\"ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline\">\n<td rowspan=\"1\" class=\"ltx_eqn_cell class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Triplet Loss:</span> The triplet loss is applied to enforce that the ground-truth event embedding <math id=\"S5.SS5.SSS2.p6.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\mathbf{P}^{GT}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐏</mi><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msup><annotation id=\"S5.SS5.SSS2.p6.m3\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\mathbf{P}^{CF}_{i}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mi>F</mi></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathbf{P}^{CF}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, by a margin <math id=\"S5.SS5.SSS2.p6.m4\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\alpha\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> (set to 1.0):</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S5.SS5.SSS2.p7\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<table id=\"S5.E17\" class=\"ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table\">\n\n<tbody><tr class=\"ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline\">\n<td rowspan=\"1\" class=\"ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left\">(17)</span></td>\n<td class=\"ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft\"></td>\n<td class=\"ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center\"><math id=\"S5.E17.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\mathcal{L}_{\\text{Causal-TL}}=\\max\\big(0,d(\\mathbf{P}^{GT},\\mathbf{T})-d(\\mathbf{P}^{CF}_{i},\\mathbf{T})+\\alpha\\big),\" display=\"block\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class=\"ltx_font_mathcaligraphic\">ℒ</mi><mtext>Causal-TL</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize=\"1.200em\" minsize=\"1.200em\">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><msup><mi>𝐏</mi><mrow><mi>G</mi><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐓</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐏</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mi>F</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>𝐓</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>α</mi></mrow><mo maxsize=\"1.200em\" minsize=\"1.200em\">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathcal{L}_{\\text{Causal-TL}}=\\max\\big(0,d(\\mathbf{P}^{GT},\\mathbf{T})-d(\\mathbf{P}^{CF}_{i},\\mathbf{T})+\\alpha\\big),</annotation></semantics></math></td>\n<td class=\"ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright\"></td></tr></tbody>\n</table>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S5.SS5.SSS2.p8\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S5.SS5.SSS2.p8.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">where <math id=\"S5.SS5.SSS2.p8.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"d(\\cdot,\\cdot)\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">⋅</mo><mo rspace=\"0em\">,</mo><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">⋅</mo><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">d(\\cdot,\\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the distance between two embeddings (e.g., cosine similarity or Euclidean distance). This loss function encourages the model to capture the causal relationships between events and time-series movements by penalizing counterfactual events that deviate from the causal signal of the ground-truth event.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S5.SS5.SSS2.p9\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S5.SS5.SSS2.p9.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The combination of diverse counterfactual sampling and causal learning ensures that CAMEF effectively learns the true causal drivers of financial market movements, improving its robustness and predictive power.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S5.SS5.SSS2.p10\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S5.SS5.SSS2.p10.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S5.SS5.SSS2.p10.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Total Loss:</span> The overall training loss for CAMEF is defined as:</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S5.SS5.SSS2.p11\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<table id=\"S5.E18\" class=\"ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table\">\n\n<tbody><tr class=\"ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline\">\n<td rowspan=\"1\" class=\"ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_left\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_left\">(18)</span></td>\n<td class=\"ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft\"></td>\n<td class=\"ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center\"><math id=\"S5.E18.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\mathcal{L}_{\\text{Total}}=\\mathcal{L}_{\\text{Time}}+\\mathcal{L}_{\\text{Causal-TL}},\" display=\"block\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class=\"ltx_font_mathcaligraphic\">ℒ</mi><mtext>Total</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi class=\"ltx_font_mathcaligraphic\">ℒ</mi><mtext>Time</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi class=\"ltx_font_mathcaligraphic\">ℒ</mi><mtext>Causal-TL</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathcal{L}_{\\text{Total}}=\\mathcal{L}_{\\text{Time}}+\\mathcal{L}_{\\text{Causal-TL}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>\n<td class=\"ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright\"></td></tr></tbody>\n</table>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S5.SS5.SSS2.p12\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S5.SS5.SSS2.p12.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">where <math id=\"S5.SS5.SSS2.p12.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\mathcal{L}_{\\text{Time}}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><msub><mi class=\"ltx_font_mathcaligraphic\">ℒ</mi><mtext>Time</mtext></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathcal{L}_{\\text{Time}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the objective for time series forecasting, as defined in Equation <a href=\"#S5.E14\" title=\"In 5.4. Time-Series Forecasting Post-Regressor and Learning Objectives ‣ 5. CAMEF Architecture ‣ CAMEF: Causal-Augmented Multi-Modality Event-Driven Financial Forecasting by Integrating Time Series Patterns and Salient Macroeconomic Announcements\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">14</span></a>.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S6\" class=\"ltx_section\">\n<h2 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_section\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_section\">6. </span>Experiments</h2>\n\n<div id=\"S6.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S6.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">In this section, we evaluate CAMEF by addressing the following key questions: <span id=\"S6.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">RQ1. Accuracy:</span> How accurately does CAMEF forecast fina ncial market based on events? <span id=\"S6.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">RQ2. Model Effectiveness:</span> How do different components enhance CAMEF’s predictive performance? <span id=\"S6.p1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">RQ3. Event Analysis:</span> Which types of events exhibit stronger influences to financial market?</p>\n</div>\n<section id=\"S6.SS1\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">6.1. </span>Experimental Settings</h3>\n\n<section id=\"S6.SS1.SSS1\" class=\"ltx_subsubsection\">\n<h4 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection\">6.1.1. </span>Datasets.</h4>\n\n<div id=\"S6.SS1.SSS1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S6.SS1.SSS1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">We utilized the collected event scripts and time-series data as outlined in Sec. <a href=\"#S4\" title=\"4. Data Collection and Counterfactual Event Augmentation ‣ CAMEF: Causal-Augmented Multi-Modality Event-Driven Financial Forecasting by Integrating Time Series Patterns and Salient Macroeconomic Announcements\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">4</span></a> and detailed in Appendix B. The dataset was divided into training, validation, and testing sets in a 6:2:2 ratio. The training set was used to train the models, while the validation set was used for convergence checking and early stopping to prevent overfitting. The final results, based on the test set, are reported in Table <a href=\"#S5.T2\" title=\"Table 2 ‣ 5.4. Time-Series Forecasting Post-Regressor and Learning Objectives ‣ 5. CAMEF Architecture ‣ CAMEF: Causal-Augmented Multi-Modality Event-Driven Financial Forecasting by Integrating Time Series Patterns and Salient Macroeconomic Announcements\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2</span></a>.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S6.SS1.SSS2\" class=\"ltx_subsubsection\">\n<h4 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection\">6.1.2. </span>Baselines.</h4>\n\n<div id=\"S6.SS1.SSS2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S6.SS1.SSS2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">To evaluate our proposed method, we compare it against both <span id=\"S6.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">uni-modal</span> and <span id=\"S6.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">multi-modal</span> time series forecasting approaches. For the <span id=\"S6.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">uni-modal baselines</span>, we considered the traditional yet robust ARIMA model <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib7\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Box and Jenkins, 1994</a>)</cite>, the linear neural model DLinear <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib60\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Zeng et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, and several state-of-the-art transformer-based time-series models, including AutoFormer <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib9\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Chen et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, FEDformer <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib62\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Zhou et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, and iTransformer <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib31\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Liu et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>. For the <span id=\"S6.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.4\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">multi-modal baselines</span>, we included TEST <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib52\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Sun et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and GPT4MTS <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib25\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Jia et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S6.SS1.SSS3\" class=\"ltx_subsubsection\">\n<h4 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection\">6.1.3. </span>Test Settings</h4>\n\n<div id=\"S6.SS1.SSS3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S6.SS1.SSS3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">We evaluate the baselines and CAMEF across three time horizons—short, medium, and long run, to simulate real investment behavior. For each aligned pair of event and time-series data <math id=\"S6.SS1.SSS3.p1.m1\" class=\"ltx_math_unparsed\" alttext=\"([\\mathcal{X}_{i-\\tau:i+\\tau}\\mapsto\\mathcal{E}_{i}])\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">[</mo><msub><mi class=\"ltx_font_mathcaligraphic\">𝒳</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mo lspace=\"0.278em\" rspace=\"0.278em\">:</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></mrow></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\">↦</mo><msub><mi class=\"ltx_font_mathcaligraphic\">ℰ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\">]</mo></mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">([\\mathcal{X}_{i-\\tau:i+\\tau}\\mapsto\\mathcal{E}_{i}])</annotation></semantics></math> as defined in Sec. <a href=\"#S3\" title=\"3. Problem Formulation ‣ CAMEF: Causal-Augmented Multi-Modality Event-Driven Financial Forecasting by Integrating Time Series Patterns and Salient Macroeconomic Announcements\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">3</span></a>, we use the event script (<math id=\"S6.SS1.SSS3.p1.m2\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\mathcal{X}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi class=\"ltx_font_mathcaligraphic\">𝒳</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathcal{X}</annotation></semantics></math>) and the time-series segment preceding the event time point <math id=\"S6.SS1.SSS3.p1.m3\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"i\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">i</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e., <math id=\"S6.SS1.SSS3.p1.m4\" class=\"ltx_math_unparsed\" alttext=\"\\mathcal{X}_{i-\\tau:i}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mi class=\"ltx_font_mathcaligraphic\">𝒳</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mo lspace=\"0.278em\" rspace=\"0.278em\">:</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathcal{X}_{i-\\tau:i}</annotation></semantics></math>, to forecast the future time-series segment <math id=\"S6.SS1.SSS3.p1.m5\" class=\"ltx_math_unparsed\" alttext=\"\\mathcal{X}_{i+1:i+\\tau}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mi class=\"ltx_font_mathcaligraphic\">𝒳</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo lspace=\"0.278em\" rspace=\"0.278em\">:</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathcal{X}_{i+1:i+\\tau}</annotation></semantics></math>. The value of <math id=\"S6.SS1.SSS3.p1.m6\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\tau\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\tau</annotation></semantics></math> is adjusted based on the time horizon: we set <math id=\"S6.SS1.SSS3.p1.m7\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\tau\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\tau</annotation></semantics></math> to 35, 70, and 140 for short, medium, and long-term forecasts, respectively. These correspond to 175 minutes (about half a trading day), 350 minutes (about one trading day), and 700 minutes (about two trading days).</p>\n</div>\n<figure id=\"S6.T3\" class=\"ltx_table\">\n<figcaption class=\"ltx_caption\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_table\"><span id=\"S6.T3.3\" class=\"ltx_text\" style=\"font-size:90%;\">Table 3</span>. </span><span id=\"S6.T3.4\" class=\"ltx_text\" style=\"font-size:90%;\">Ablation Study Results (MSE) Evaluating the CAMEF Model Components at Forecasting Lengths of 35, 70, and 140.</span></figcaption>\n<div class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection\">6.1.4. </span>Implementation Overview</h4>\n\n<div id=\"S6.SS1.SSS4.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S6.SS1.SSS4.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">For the single-modality approaches (ARIMA, DLinear, AutoFormer, FEDformer, iTransformer, and PatchTST), we tested two methods: (1) training the models on continuous historical time-series data and testing on aligned event-based time-series segments from the test set, and (2) training the models directly on event-based time-series segments, and also test on the aligned event-based time-series segments from the test set. The second approach produced more accurate results, and these are the results presented in this paper. Specifically, for each aligned event data pair <math id=\"S6.SS1.SSS4.p1.m1\" class=\"ltx_math_unparsed\" alttext=\"([\\mathcal{X}_{i-\\tau:i+\\tau}\\mapsto\\mathcal{E}_{i}])\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">[</mo><msub><mi class=\"ltx_font_mathcaligraphic\">𝒳</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mo lspace=\"0.278em\" rspace=\"0.278em\">:</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></mrow></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\">↦</mo><msub><mi class=\"ltx_font_mathcaligraphic\">ℰ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\">]</mo></mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">([\\mathcal{X}_{i-\\tau:i+\\tau}\\mapsto\\mathcal{E}_{i}])</annotation></semantics></math>, single-modality approaches use only the time-series segment preceding the event, <math id=\"S6.SS1.SSS4.p1.m2\" class=\"ltx_math_unparsed\" alttext=\"\\mathcal{X}_{i-\\tau:i}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mi class=\"ltx_font_mathcaligraphic\">𝒳</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mo lspace=\"0.278em\" rspace=\"0.278em\">:</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathcal{X}_{i-\\tau:i}</annotation></semantics></math>, to train the models and forecast the subsequent segment, <math id=\"S6.SS1.SSS4.p1.m3\" class=\"ltx_math_unparsed\" alttext=\"\\mathcal{X}_{i+1:i+\\tau}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mi class=\"ltx_font_mathcaligraphic\">𝒳</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo lspace=\"0.278em\" rspace=\"0.278em\">:</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathcal{X}_{i+1:i+\\tau}</annotation></semantics></math>; and testing follows the same approach. Detailed settings for each model are provided in Appendix C.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S6.SS1.SSS4.p2\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S6.SS1.SSS4.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">For the multi-modality approaches (GPT4MTS, TEST, and CAMEF), both the event script <math id=\"S6.SS1.SSS4.p2.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\mathcal{E}_{i}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><msub><mi class=\"ltx_font_mathcaligraphic\">ℰ</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathcal{E}_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and the time-series segment preceding the event, <math id=\"S6.SS1.SSS4.p2.m2\" class=\"ltx_math_unparsed\" alttext=\"\\mathcal{X}_{i-\\tau:i}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mi class=\"ltx_font_mathcaligraphic\">𝒳</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mo lspace=\"0.278em\" rspace=\"0.278em\">:</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathcal{X}_{i-\\tau:i}</annotation></semantics></math>, are used as input to train the models to forecast the post-event time-series segment, <math id=\"S6.SS1.SSS4.p2.m3\" class=\"ltx_math_unparsed\" alttext=\"\\mathcal{X}_{i+1:i+\\tau}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mi class=\"ltx_font_mathcaligraphic\">𝒳</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo lspace=\"0.278em\" rspace=\"0.278em\">:</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathcal{X}_{i+1:i+\\tau}</annotation></semantics></math>. Implementation details, including model configurations and training settings, are explained in Appendix C.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S6.SS2\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">6.2. </span>Experimental Results for Event-Driven Time-Series Forecasting (RQ1)</h3>\n\n<div id=\"S6.SS2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S6.SS2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Table <a href=\"#S5.T2\" title=\"Table 2 ‣ 5.4. Time-Series Forecasting Post-Regressor and Learning Objectives ‣ 5. CAMEF Architecture ‣ CAMEF: Causal-Augmented Multi-Modality Event-Driven Financial Forecasting by Integrating Time Series Patterns and Salient Macroeconomic Announcements\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2</span></a> presents the forecasting results for the five datasets across short, medium, and long forecasting horizons. CAMEF outperformed other models in 24 out of 30 settings, achieving first-place rankings, and ranked second in the remaining 6 settings. Specifically, CAMEF demonstrated the best performance across all forecasting lengths for the Stock Market Indices (SPX, INDU, and NDX), except for short-horizon forecasting on INDU, highlighting its effectiveness in event-driven stock market forecasting. For treasury bonds, CAMEF achieved the best results across all forecasting lengths for the 1-month treasury bond (USGG1M) and ranked second for the 5-year treasury bond (USGG5YR). The slightly lower performance on USGG5YR suggests that long-run treasury bonds may be less sensitive to event-driven factors and more influenced by historical trends.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S6.SS2.p2\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S6.SS2.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Compared to single-modality models (e.g., DLinear, Autoformer, FEDformer, PatchTST, and iTransformer), CAMEF achieved an average MSE reduction of 62.55% relative to the best-performing single-modality model, iTransformer. Among multi-modality models, CAMEF surpassed TEST, the second-best performer, with an average MSE reduction of 33.55%.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S6.SS2.p3\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S6.SS2.p3.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">These results highlight three key insights: (1) effectively leveraging multi-modality information provides significant performance gains, particularly for SPX, INDU, NDX, and USGG1M; (2) transformer-based methods consistently outperform classical models such as ARIMA; and (3) CAMEF’s superior training and feature fusion strategies establish it as the most effective method for event-driven financial forecasting tasks.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S6.SS3\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">6.3. </span>Ablation Studies on Model Components (RQ2)</h3>\n\n<div id=\"S6.SS3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S6.SS3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">To evaluate the effectiveness of each component in CAMEF, we conduct comprehensive ablation studies on Textual Modality, Causal Learning, Feature Fusion, GPT2 Decoder, and the Post-Regressor. Based on the full CAMEF model, we remove the corresponding neural layers, such as the RoBERTa encoder for textual modality or the causal learning component, to assess their individual contributions. The ablation results are presented in Table <a href=\"#S6.T3\" title=\"Table 3 ‣ 6.1.3. Test Settings ‣ 6.1. Experimental Settings ‣ 6. Experiments ‣ CAMEF: Causal-Augmented Multi-Modality Event-Driven Financial Forecasting by Integrating Time Series Patterns and Salient Macroeconomic Announcements\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">3</span></a>, where the left part of the table uses ✓ or ✗ to indicate whether the specific component is included or excluded in the test. From the results, three key findings are: (1) The full CAMEF model achieves the best performance across all datasets, demonstrating the critical importance of utilizing both textual and time-series modalities; (2) Causal learning provides incremental improvements, confirming its value in capturing cause-effect relationships within the data; (3) The proposed feature fusion layers and GPT2 decoder effectively integrate and leverage multi-modality features, significantly enhancing the model’s ability to decode time-series data. These findings underscore the necessity of each component in achieving optimal performance for event-driven financial forecasting tasks.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S6.SS4\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">6.4. </span>Ablation Studies on Different Type of Events (RQ3)</h3>\n\n<div id=\"S6.SS4.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S6.SS4.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Table <a href=\"#S6.T4\" title=\"Table 4 ‣ 6.1.3. Test Settings ‣ 6.1. Experimental Settings ‣ 6. Experiments ‣ CAMEF: Causal-Augmented Multi-Modality Event-Driven Financial Forecasting by Integrating Time Series Patterns and Salient Macroeconomic Announcements\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">4</span></a> shows the predictive performance of different events on the S&amp;P500 Index. <span id=\"S6.SS4.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">FOMC Minutes</span> achieve the lowest MSE and MAE, confirming their critical importance for market prediction. <span id=\"S6.SS4.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Unemployment Insurance Claims</span> and <span id=\"S6.SS4.p1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Unemployment Situation Reports</span> also come with lower errors than the full selection, however the latter becomes less effective at long forecasting length. In contrast, <span id=\"S6.SS4.p1.1.4\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">CPI</span> and <span id=\"S6.SS4.p1.1.5\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">PPI Reports</span> show weaker predictive power, with PPI yielding the highest errors and CPI improving slightly at long forecasting length. These results emphasize the importance of FOMC and unemployment-related events for financial forecasting.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S6.SS5\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">6.5. </span>Parameter Sensitivity Analysis</h3>\n\n<figure id=\"S6.F4\" class=\"ltx_figure\">\n<div class=\"ltx_flex_figure\">\n<div class=\"ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2\">\n<figure id=\"S6.F4.sf1\" class=\"ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center\"><img src=\"2502.04592v3/figures/camef_sensitivity_alpha.png\" id=\"S6.F4.sf1.g1\" class=\"ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape\" style=\"aspect-ratio:476/357;\" width=\"476\" height=\"357\" alt=\"Refer to caption\">\n<figcaption class=\"ltx_caption ltx_centering\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure\"><span id=\"S6.F4.sf1.3\" class=\"ltx_text\" style=\"font-size:90%;\">(a)</span> </span><span id=\"S6.F4.sf1.4\" class=\"ltx_text\" style=\"font-size:90%;\">Effect of counterfactual sample size (<math id=\"S6.F4.sf1.m2\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\alpha\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>)</span></figcaption>\n</figure></div><div class=\"ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2\">\n<figure id=\"S6.F4.sf2\" class=\"ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center\"><img src=\"2502.04592v3/figures/camef_sensitivity_k.png\" id=\"S6.F4.sf2.g1\" class=\"ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape\" style=\"aspect-ratio:476/357;\" width=\"476\" height=\"357\" alt=\"Refer to caption\">\n<figcaption class=\"ltx_caption ltx_centering\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure\"><span id=\"S6.F4.sf2.3\" class=\"ltx_text\" style=\"font-size:90%;\">(b)</span> </span><span id=\"S6.F4.sf2.4\" class=\"ltx_text\" style=\"font-size:90%;\">Effect of post-regressor depth (<math id=\"S6.F4.sf2.m2\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"k\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">k</annotation></semantics></math>)</span></figcaption>\n</figure></div></div>\n<figcaption class=\"ltx_caption ltx_centering\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure\"><span id=\"S6.F4.3\" class=\"ltx_text\" style=\"font-size:90%;\">Figure 4</span>. </span><span id=\"S6.F4.4\" class=\"ltx_text\" style=\"font-size:90%;\">Sensitivity analysis of CAMEF on the SP500 dataset with respect to key hyperparameters.</span></figcaption>\n</figure>\n<div id=\"S6.SS5.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S6.SS5.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">We examine the impact of two key hyperparameters in CAMEF on SPX dataset with 35 predictive length: the number of counterfactual samples (<math id=\"S6.SS5.p1.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\alpha\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>) and the depth of the post-regressor network (<math id=\"S6.SS5.p1.m2\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"k\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">k</annotation></semantics></math>). The number of GPT-2 layers (<math id=\"S6.SS5.p1.m3\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"l\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">l</annotation></semantics></math>) remains fixed, as we adopt the pre-trained model without modification. As shown in Figure <a href=\"#S6.F4\" title=\"Figure 4 ‣ 6.5. Parameter Sensitivity Analysis ‣ 6. Experiments ‣ CAMEF: Causal-Augmented Multi-Modality Event-Driven Financial Forecasting by Integrating Time Series Patterns and Salient Macroeconomic Announcements\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">4</span></a>, increasing <math id=\"S6.SS5.p1.m4\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\alpha\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\alpha</annotation></semantics></math> enhances forecasting accuracy through stronger contrastive supervision, with performance gains saturating around <math id=\"S6.SS5.p1.m5\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\alpha=10\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\alpha=10</annotation></semantics></math>. Similarly, increasing <math id=\"S6.SS5.p1.m6\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"k\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">k</annotation></semantics></math> improves decoding capacity, though with diminishing returns beyond <math id=\"S6.SS5.p1.m7\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"k=4\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">k=4</annotation></semantics></math>. These trends suggest that CAMEF performs robustly across a range of configurations, benefiting from moderate complexity increases without overfitting.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S7\" class=\"ltx_section\">\n<h2 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_section\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_section\">7. </span>Conclusion and Future Work</h2>\n\n<div id=\"S7.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S7.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">This paper proposed <span id=\"S7.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">CAMEF</span>, a multi-modality model for event-driven financial forecasting, which integrates effective causal learning and an LLM-based counterfactual event augmentation strategy. Alongside the model, we introduced a novel synthetic dataset comprising 6 types of salient macroeconomic event scripts, their counterfactual samples, and high-frequency time-series data for 5 key financial assets, aligned with real-world investment practices. Extensive experiments demonstrated CAMEF’s superior predictive performance compared to prior deep time-series and multi-modality methods. Ablation studies testified the importance of causal learning and other designed components of CAMEF. Additionally, it is found that FOMC and unemployment-related events provided the most predictive value among the tested event types.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S7.p2\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"S7.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">For future work, we plan to leverage advanced LLMs for enhanced textual encoding to extract deeper semantic information, refine the cross-modality causal inference mechanisms, and expand the dataset to include additional event types, such as political events and corporate market-sensitive news.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"Sx1\" class=\"ltx_section\">\n<h2 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_section\">Acknowledgements</h2>\n\n<div id=\"Sx1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"Sx1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">This work was supported in part by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (NSFC) under Grant Nos. 62402396 and 72471197. We would like to thank the anonymous reviewers for their valuable comments and suggestions that helped improve the quality of this paper.</p>\n</div>\n<div class=\"ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage\"></div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"bib\" class=\"ltx_bibliography\">\n<h2 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_bibliography\">References</h2>\n\n<ul class=\"ltx_biblist\">\n      \n<li id=\"bib.bib2\" class=\"ltx_bibitem\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_role_refnum ltx_tag_bibitem\">Ariyo et al<span id=\"bib.bib2.2\" class=\"ltx_text\">.</span> ([n. d.])</span>\n<span class=\"ltx_bibblock\">\nAdebiyi A. 1 = Strongly Negative; 2 = Very; Negative; 3 = Moderate Negative; 4 = Slightly Negative; 5 = Neutral; 6 = Slightly Positive; 7 = Moderate Positive; 8 = Very Positive; 9 = Strongly Positive; 10 = Extremely Positive\n{<span id=\"A1.SS2.p2.pic1.2.1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_italic\">text_type</span>} summary: {<span id=\"A1.SS2.p2.pic1.2.1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_italic\">text</span>}\n<br class=\"ltx_break\">Output the sentiment analysis as:\n<br class=\"ltx_break\">Sentiment rating: (0 to 10), Explanation:</span></span>\n</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"A1.SS3\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">A.3. </span>Counterfactual Event Generation Prompt Template</h3>\n\n<div id=\"A1.SS3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A1.SS3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">To generate counterfactual versions of a text with different sentiment levels, we use a prompt that instructs the model to modify key facts and information to align with a target sentiment rating. The model is provided with the original sentiment rating and sentiment description and is asked to adjust the text to reflect a specified target sentiment rating. Below is the prompt, where the text within “{ }” indicates the input variables:</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A1.SS3.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\"><span class=\"ltx_inline-block\"><svg width=\"434.07\"><span class=\"ltx_foreignobject_container\"><span class=\"ltx_foreignobject_content\">\n<span id=\"A1.SS3.p2.pic1.2\" class=\"ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom\" style=\"width:31.37em;\">\n<span id=\"A1.SS3.p2.pic1.2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"A1.SS3.p2.pic1.2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text\" style=\"--ltx-fg-color:#000000;\">The original text has been identified with a sentiment rating of {<span id=\"A1.SS3.p2.pic1.2.1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_italic\">current_sentiment_rating</span>} ({<span id=\"A1.SS3.p2.pic1.2.1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_italic\">current_sentiment</span>}).\n<br class=\"ltx_break\">Your task is to generate a counterfactual version of the text that aligns with a sentiment rating of {<span id=\"A1.SS3.p2.pic1.2.1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_italic\">target_sentiment_rating</span>} ({<span id=\"A1.SS3.p2.pic1.2.1.1.4\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_italic\">target_sentiment</span>}) by modifying the key facts and information to reflect the specified target sentiment score about the economy, while keep the overall format and the sentiment-neural content unchanged.\n<br class=\"ltx_break\">Original text: {<span id=\"A1.SS3.p2.pic1.2.1.1.5\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_italic\">original_text</span>}\n<br class=\"ltx_break\">Counterfactual text with a sentiment rating of {<span id=\"A1.SS3.p2.pic1.2.1.1.6\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_italic\">target_sentiment_rating</span>} ({<span id=\"A1.SS3.p2.pic1.2.1.1.7\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_italic\">target_sentiment</span>}):</span></span>\n</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>\n</div>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"A2\" class=\"ltx_appendix\">\n<h2 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_appendix\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix\">Appendix B </span>Implementation Details of Dataset Collection and Preprocessing</h2>\n\n<section id=\"A2.SS1\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">B.1. </span>Dataset Collection</h3>\n\n<div id=\"A2.SS1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A2.SS1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">To construct the CAMEF dataset, raw macroeconomic event data are crawled from official government sources (Tab. <a href=\"#S2.T1\" title=\"Table 1 ‣ 2.3. Counterfactual Data Augmentation by LLMs ‣ 2. Related Work ‣ CAMEF: Causal-Augmented Multi-Modality Event-Driven Financial Forecasting by Integrating Time Series Patterns and Salient Macroeconomic Announcements\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">1</span></a>) in various formats (PDF, HTML, TXT). We utilize the following Python libraries:</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A2.SS1.p2\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<ul id=\"A2.I1\" class=\"ltx_itemize\">\n<li id=\"A2.I1.i1\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"A2.I1.i1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A2.I1.i1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"A2.I1.i1.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Requests</span> – to send HTTP requests for archive access;</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"A2.I1.i2\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"A2.I1.i2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A2.I1.i2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"A2.I1.i2.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Selenium</span> – to locate and download files via HTML headers;</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"A2.I1.i3\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"A2.I1.i3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A2.I1.i3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"A2.I1.i3.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">BeautifulSoup</span> – to parse HTML and extract file links.</p>\n</div></li>\n</ul>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A2.SS1.p3\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A2.SS1.p3.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The dataset covers six event types: FOMC minutes, CPI, PPI, unemployment insurance, unemployment rate, and GDP advance releases.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"A2.SS2\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">B.2. </span>Preprocessing</h3>\n\n<div id=\"A2.SS2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A2.SS2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Raw files are converted into a unified text format. <span id=\"A2.SS2.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">PyPDF2</span> and <span id=\"A2.SS2.p1.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">pdfplumber</span> extract content from PDFs, while <span id=\"A2.SS2.p1.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter\">BeautifulSoup</span> parses HTML using depth-first traversal. TXT files are used as-is. We convert all the tables into structured text using the delimiter “|”, as shown:</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A2.SS2.p2\" class=\"ltx_para\"><pre id=\"A2.SS2.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_verbatim ltx_font_typewriter\">&lt;Table&gt;\nHeader 1 | Header 2 | Header 3\n----\nCell 1  | Cell 2    | Cell 3\n&lt;/Table&gt;\n</pre>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A2.SS2.p3\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A2.SS2.p3.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">This preprocessing ensures clean, consistent, machine-readable data, supporting robust analysis and model training.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"A3\" class=\"ltx_appendix\">\n<h2 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_appendix\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix\">Appendix C </span>Implementation Details</h2>\n\n<div id=\"A3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Single-modality baselines (ARIMA, DLinear, AutoFormer, FEDFormer, iTransformer, PatchTST) were adapted from Time-Series-Library to the event-driven setting, using pre-event segments to predict 35-, 70-, and 140-step trends. All models were trained for 10 epochs with batch size 32.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A3.p2\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A3.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">For multi-modality baselines, we used TEST and a re-implemented GPT4MTS (with LongFormer replacing BERT). Both were aligned to the same forecasting horizons and training settings.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A3.p3\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A3.p3.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">CAMEF followed a two-stage pipeline: MOMENT was pre-trained on time series, then the full model fine-tuned on aligned text–series pairs. MOMENT and RoBERTa (excluding final layer) were frozen, while GPT2 and fusion layers were trainable, enabling robust multimodal forecasting.</p>\n</div>\n<section id=\"A3.SS1\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">C.1. </span>Implementation of Baseline Models</h3>\n\n<div id=\"A3.SS1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A3.SS1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Baseline models were developed with objectives distinct from our event-driven forecasting approach, as single-modality methods are primarily designed for continuous time-series forecasting. To enable a fair comparison, we adapted these models to align with an event-driven context, where past time-series data preceding an event is used to forecast trends within a defined forecasting horizon.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A3.SS1.p2\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A3.SS1.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"A3.SS1.p2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Single-Modality Models:</span> For time-series-based single-modality models, including <span id=\"A3.SS1.p2.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">DLinear, AutoFormer, FEDFormer, iTransformer, and PatchTST</span>, we utilized the open-source library <span id=\"A3.SS1.p2.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Time-Series-Library<span id=\"footnote2\" class=\"ltx_note ltx_role_footnote\"><sup class=\"ltx_note_mark\">2</sup><span class=\"ltx_note_outer\"><span class=\"ltx_note_content\"><sup class=\"ltx_note_mark\">2</sup>\n                <span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_note\"><span id=\"footnote2.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_medium\">2</span></span>\n                \n                \n                \n              <a href=\"https://github.com/thuml/Time-Series-Library\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_medium\">https://github.com/thuml/Time-Series-Library</a></span></span></span></span>. Time-series segments were extracted with lengths covering both the input and forecasting periods surrounding each event, ensuring alignment with the respective event’s time step. The input segment represents the historical trend information, while the forecasting period is treated as \"unseen\" data to be predicted. Input and forecasting lengths were consistently set to 35, 70, and 140 time steps across all experiments, as described in Sec. <a href=\"#S6.SS1\" title=\"6.1. Experimental Settings ‣ 6. Experiments ‣ CAMEF: Causal-Augmented Multi-Modality Event-Driven Financial Forecasting by Integrating Time Series Patterns and Salient Macroeconomic Announcements\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">6.1</span></a>. All models were trained for 10 epochs, with a batch size of 32. These settings ensured convergence of the loss function and maintained consistency with CAMEF’s training configuration.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A3.SS1.p3\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A3.SS1.p3.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"A3.SS1.p3.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Multi-Modality Models:</span> For multi-modality methods, including <span id=\"A3.SS1.p3.1.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">TEST</span> and <span id=\"A3.SS1.p3.1.3\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">GPT4MTS</span>, we followed implementation strategies specific to each model.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A3.SS1.p4\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<ul id=\"A3.I1\" class=\"ltx_itemize\">\n<li id=\"A3.I1.i1\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"A3.I1.i1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A3.I1.i1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"A3.I1.i1.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">TEST:</span> We followed the instructions provided in the open-source TEST repository<span id=\"footnote3\" class=\"ltx_note ltx_role_footnote\"><sup class=\"ltx_note_mark\">3</sup><span class=\"ltx_note_outer\"><span class=\"ltx_note_content\"><sup class=\"ltx_note_mark\">3</sup>\n                    <span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_note\">3</span>\n                    \n                    \n                    \n                  <a href=\"https://github.com/SCXsunchenxi/TEST\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter\">https://github.com/SCXsunchenxi/TEST</a></span></span></span>, which involved two training stages. In the first stage, the encoder was trained by selecting 10 prototype words based on GPT vocabulary clustering (as instructed in the repository) to align textual representations with time-series data. The second stage involved training the time-series decoder, where input and forecasting steps were set to 35, 70, and 140, similar to the single-modality models. The batch size was set to 7, and training epochs were kept at 10.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"A3.I1.i2\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"A3.I1.i2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A3.I1.i2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"A3.I1.i2.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">GPT4MTS:</span> As the official implementation of GPT4MTS was unavailable, we re-implemented the model based on its original paper. Instead of using BERT <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib13\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Devlin et al., 2019</a>)</cite> as the textual encoder, we employed LongFormer <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep\">(<a href=\"#bib.bib5\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">Beltagy et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, which is better suited for encoding longer contexts, as our texts tend to be relatively lengthy. Input time-series segments were used to forecast the time-series data at the forecasting lengths of 35, 70, and 140. We kept training epochs at 10 and the batch size at 7 to ensure consistency with other baselines.</p>\n</div></li>\n</ul>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"A3.SS2\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">C.2. </span>Implementation of CAMEF</h3>\n\n<figure id=\"A3.T5\" class=\"ltx_table\">\n<figcaption class=\"ltx_caption ltx_centering\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_table\"><span id=\"A3.T5.3\" class=\"ltx_text\" style=\"font-size:90%;\">Table 5</span>. </span><span id=\"A3.T5.4\" class=\"ltx_text\" style=\"font-size:90%;\">Learning Rates for CAMEF Components</span></figcaption>\n<div id=\"A3.T5.5\" class=\"ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer\" encoding=\"application/x-tex\">1\\times 10^{-5}</annotation></semantics></math></td></tr>\n</table>\n</span></div>\n</figure>\n<div id=\"A3.SS2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"A3.SS2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The batch size is set to 10, and the training epochs are set to 10, consistent with the baseline models.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A3.SS2.p2\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A3.SS2.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The implementation of <span id=\"A3.SS2.p2.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">CAMEF</span> involves two distinct training stages to ensure effective learning of both time-series and textual features, while leveraging pre-trained components:</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A3.SS2.p3\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<ol id=\"A3.I2\" class=\"ltx_enumerate\">\n<li id=\"A3.I2.i1\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">(1)</span> \n<div id=\"A3.I2.i1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A3.I2.i1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"A3.I2.i1.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Pre-training MOMENT:</span> In the first stage, we pre-train the MOMENT model using the time-series segments from the training data. This step focuses on learning representations of the past time-series patterns.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"A3.I2.i2\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">(2)</span> \n<div id=\"A3.I2.i2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A3.I2.i2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"A3.I2.i2.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Training Entire CAMEF:</span> In the second stage, we train the entire CAMEF model using both event scripts and their corresponding aligned time-series segments. During this stage, certain parameters are frozen to retain the pre-trained knowledge, while others remain open for fine-tuning:</p>\n<ul id=\"A3.I2.i2.I1\" class=\"ltx_itemize\">\n<li id=\"A3.I2.i2.I1.i1\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"A3.I2.i2.I1.i1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A3.I2.i2.I1.i1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"A3.I2.i2.I1.i1.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Frozen Parameters:</span> All parameters of the MOMENT model and RoBERTa (except for the last hidden layer) are frozen. Additionally, the token embedding layer of GPT2 in the decoder is frozen to preserve its pre-trained representations.</p>\n</div></li>\n<li id=\"A3.I2.i2.I1.i2\" class=\"ltx_item\" style=\"list-style-type:none;\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_item\">•</span> \n<div id=\"A3.I2.i2.I1.i2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A3.I2.i2.I1.i2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"A3.I2.i2.I1.i2.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Trainable Parameters:</span> The remaining components of GPT2, the last hidden layer of RoBERTa, and other components such as the embedding, residual, fusion, and output layers are open for training.</p>\n</div></li>\n</ul>\n</div></li>\n</ol>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A3.SS2.p4\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A3.SS2.p4.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The hidden sizes of the different components of the CAMEF model are detailed in Sec. <a href=\"#S5\" title=\"5. CAMEF Architecture ‣ CAMEF: Causal-Augmented Multi-Modality Event-Driven Financial Forecasting by Integrating Time Series Patterns and Salient Macroeconomic Announcements\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">5</span></a>. To optimize the model effectively, we adopt component-specific learning rates as listed in Table <a href=\"#A3.T5\" title=\"Table 5 ‣ C.2. Implementation of CAMEF ‣ Appendix C Implementation Details ‣ CAMEF: Causal-Augmented Multi-Modality Event-Driven Financial Forecasting by Integrating Time Series Patterns and Salient Macroeconomic Announcements\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">5</span></a>.</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"A3.SS2.p5\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"A3.SS2.p5.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"A3.SS2.p5.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_phantom\"><span style=\"visibility:hidden\"></span></span></p>\n<p id=\"A3.SS2.p5.2\" class=\"ltx_p ltx_parbox ltx_align_top\" style=\"width:165.6pt;\">This phantom box blocks the right column.</p>\n</div>\n</section>\n</section>\n</article>\n</div>\n</div>\n<footer class=\"arxiv-html-footer\">\n  <div class=\"ltx_page_logo\">\n    Experimental support, please\n    <a href=\"./2502.04592v3/__stdout.txt\" class=\"ltx_ref\"\n    target=\"_blank\" rel=\"nofollow\">view the build logs</a>\n    for errors. Implementation of CAMEF\n License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license\narXiv:2502.04592v3 [cs.LG] 08 Aug 2025\nCAMEF: Causal-Augmented Multi-Modality Event-Driven Financial Forecasting by Integrating Time Series Patterns and Salient Macroeconomic Announcements\nConference: Proceedings of the 31st ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining V.2; August 3–7, 2025; Toronto, ON, CanadaProceedings of the 31st ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining V.2 (KDD ’25), August 3–7, 2025, Toronto, ON, CanadaDOI: 10.1145/3711896.3736872ISBN: 979-8-4007-1454-2/2025/08CCS: Applied computing EconomicsCCS: Computing methodologies Neural networks\nYang Zhang\nNote: Corresponding authors.\nAffiliation: Southwestern University of Finance and Economics, Chengdu, China\nemail: zhang.yang.r54@kyoto-u.jp\n, \nWenbo Yang\nAffiliation: Southwestern University of Finance and Economics, Chengdu, China\nemail: 223081200030@smail.swufe.edu.cn\n, \nJun Wang\nAffiliation: Southwestern University of Finance and Economics, Chengdu, China\nemail: wangjun1987@swufe.edu.cn\n, \nQiang Ma\nAffiliation: Kyoto Institute of Technology, Kyoto, Japan\nemail: qinag@kit.ac.jp\n and \nJie Xiong\nAffiliation: Southwestern University of Finance and Economics, Chengdu, China\nemail: xiongjie@swufe.edu.cn\n© acmlicensed\nAbstract.\nAccurately forecasting the impact of macroeconomic events is critical for investors and policymakers. Salient events like monetary policy decisions and employment reports often trigger market movements by shaping expectations of economic growth and risk, thereby establishing causal relationships between events and market behavior. Existing forecasting methods typically focus either on textual analysis or time-series modeling, but fail to capture the multi-modal nature of financial markets and the causal relationship between events and price movements. To address these gaps, we propose CAMEF (Causal-Augmented Multi-Modality Event-Driven Financial Forecasting), a multi-modality framework that effectively integrates textual and time-series data with a causal learning mechanism and an LLM-based counterfactual event augmentation technique for causal-enhanced financial forecasting. Our contributions include: (1) a multi-modal framework that captures causal relationships between policy texts and historical price data; (2) a new financial dataset with six types of macroeconomic releases from 2008 to April 2024, and high-frequency real trading data for five key U.S. financial assets; and (3) an LLM-based counterfactual event augmentation strategy. We compare CAMEF to state-of-the-art transformer-based time-series and multi-modal baselines, and perform ablation studies to validate the effectiveness of the causal learning mechanism and event types.\nKeywords: Multimodal learning, Causal Learning, Financial dataset, Time-series Forecasting\n1. Introduction\nThe prices of financial assets reflect all available information, according to Fama’s Efficient Market Theory (Fama, 1965; Fama et al., 1969). Major financial releases from government sectors often trigger market movements by shaping investors’ expectations and evaluations of economic conditions, asset growth potential, and associated risks. For example, during the FOMC meeting on March 16, 2020, the Fed’s emergency rate cut to 0-0.25% sharply altered investors’ economic outlook, resulting in a massive sell-off. Major indices, including the S&P 500, NASDAQ, and Dow Jones, dropped by over 10%, marking the steepest single-day decline since 1987 (Domm, 2021). These salient macroeconomic events cause reactions in financial assets, establishing causal relationships between events and financial assets. Figure 1 illustrates multiple types of events that cause financial market reactions. Therefore, accurately forecasting the causal consequences of the salient macroeconomic releases on financial market is essential, not only to help investors manage risks and maximize returns, but also to provide policymakers with valuable insights for evaluating and refining future policies.\nFigure 1. Event-Driven Forecasting Examples: (a) Market reaction to employment insurance release; (b) Market reaction during FOMC meeting; (c) Forecasting market reactions to future events.\nPrevious studies on event-driven forecasting have primarily adopted three lines of methodologies. The first line of approaches utilizes text feature-based models, where language models, ranging from self-crafted RNN-based architectures (Huynh et al., 2017; Liu, 2018; Daigo Tashiro and Sakaji, 2019; Xu and Cohen, 2018) to pre-trained transformers (Zhou et al., [n. d.]; Shah et al., 2023), embed sentiment information into text vectors, and then stock movements are predicted as a binary classification task (e.g., hawkish vs. dovish). The second line of methodology focuses on historical time-series data, treating stock price movements as a regression problem (Taylor, 2007; Cao and Tsay, 1992). Recently, transformer-based architectures have been applied for time-series prediction, including Informer (Zhou et al., 2021), FedFormer (Zhou et al., 2022), and AutoFormer (Chen et al., 2021), etc. However, both of these directions typically focus on a single modality, neglecting multi-dimensional information. The third line of research adopts a multi-modality approach, leveraging multiple types of data sources to enhance forecasting performance. For instance, studies like (Mathur et al., 2022; Ouyang et al., 2024) incorporate textual, video, and audio data from FOMC meetings alongside corresponding market movements. While these approaches show promise for event-driven financial forecasts, they face three major limitations:\n• \nData Limitation: Existing approaches predominantly focus on a single type of event, such as FOMC meetings (Shah et al., 2023; Mathur et al., 2022; Ouyang et al., 2024), while neglecting other crucial macroeconomic events like unemployment insurance releases, CPI, PPI, and GDP advance reports. Additionally, many studies rely on daily-based time-series data for financial assets (Shah et al., 2023; Mathur et al., 2022; Ouyang et al., 2024; Taylor, 2007; Cao and Tsay, 1992; Zhou et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2021), which limits their applicability and precision in real-time trading scenarios where high-frequency data is mostly adopted.\n• \nModality Limitation: Most prior studies rely on single-modality analysis, using either textual models (Huynh et al., 2017; Liu, 2018; Daigo Tashiro and Sakaji, 2019; Xu and Cohen, 2018; Zhou et al., [n. d.]; Shah et al., 2023) or time-series models (Taylor, 2007; Cao and Tsay, 1992; Zhou et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2021), which fail to integrate the complementary strengths of both modalities. While some multi-modality approaches have been proposed (Mathur et al., 2022; Ouyang et al., 2024), they often lack advanced mechanisms for feature fusion, effective decoding strategies, and causal learning, which are critical for understanding the complex interplay between event texts and market dynamics.\n• \nCausality Limitation: Existing methods (Mathur et al., 2022; Ouyang et al., 2024) fail to incorporate causal reasoning frameworks, overlooking the causal relationships between events and market reactions. Without explicitly modeling these relationships, such approaches cannot fully capture the drivers of financial market behavior, limiting their predictive robustness.\nTo address the limitations of previous studies, we propose a novel multi-modality framework, CAMEF11\n 1\n The dataset and code for CAMEF are open-sourced at: https://github.com/lakebodhi/CAMEF (causal-Augmented Multi-Modality Event-Driven Financial Forecasting). CAMEF integrates time-series and textual features through specially designed multi-feature fusion techniques, time-series decoding mechanisms, and causal learning strategies. By conducting a thorough review of financial literature, we identify six types of salient macroeconomic events for the forecasting analysis. Furthermore, the framework employs causal data augmentation powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) and a causal contrastive learning approach to enhance the causal understanding and forecast accuracy of CAMEF. This paper offers three key contributions:\n• \nNovel Dataset: We introduce a novel open-source synthetic dataset comprising 6 types of macroeconomic event scripts (ref to Tab. 1 for details) from 2008 to April 2024 through reviewing from financial literature (CIESLAK et al., 2019; Gertler and Horvath, 2018; Masciandaro et al., 2024; Rosa, 2016; Tadle, 2022; Rosa, 2013; LUCCA and MOENCH, 2015; Rosa, 2011; Pearce and Roley, 1984; Gilbert et al., 2010; Gilbert et al., 2017; Bartolini et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2004; Goldberg and Grisse, 2013), alongside intra-day _high-frequency financial data at 5-minute intervals from key U.S. stock indexes and Treasury bonds. To support causal learning, the dataset also includes counterfactual event scripts generated using our LLM-based causal argumentation prompting, making it the first to integrate policy texts, high-frequency trading data, and causally augmented content.\n• \nNovel Multi-Modality Model: We propose a novel multi-modality approach, CAMEF, that integrates time-series and textual features, incorporating specifically designed multi-feature fusion and time-series decoding networks, which have been demonstrated to be effective for forecasting. Additionally, the model includes a causal learning mechanism to enhance forecasting capability by capturing the causal relationships between events and market reactions.\n• \nCounterfactual Generation and Learning: We introduce a counterfactual data augmentation strategy to generate counterfactual event scripts based on collected macroeconomic releases. This approach leverages LLMs to create scripts with varying sentiment levels by modifying key numerical values and sentiment-relevant phrases, while preserving the original format, writing style, and neutral words of the factual reports. Counterfactual events enable CAMEF to better understand the causal relationships between events and market reactions by learning from hypothetical scenarios, thereby improving its forecasting ability.\n2. Related Work\n2.1. Event-Drive Financial Forecasting\nEvent-driven financial forecasting (Bao et al., 2025) focuses on predicting asset prices (Goldberg and Grisse, 2013; Gilbert et al., 2010) and market volatility (LUCCA and MOENCH, 2015; CIESLAK et al., 2019) based on events like macroeconomic releases (Gilbert et al., 2010), news (Liu, 2018), corporate announcements (Zhou et al., [n. d.]), and social media activity (Xu and Cohen, 2018). Three main approaches exist in this area. The first leverages text analysis to predict asset responses based on event-related text. Early works utilized TF-IDF (Pui Cheong Fung et al., 2003; Li et al., 2014) and topic models (Si et al., 2013; Nguyen et al., 2015), progressing to RNN-based models (Huynh et al., 2017; Liu, 2018) and pre-trained transformers (Zhou et al., [n. d.]; Shah et al., 2023), which capture nuanced semantics. Although these models excel at semantic extraction, they often lack integration with historical price data, crucial for holistic forecasting.\nThe second line of approaches uses statistical and sequential models on numerical data, such as linear regression (Bhuriya et al., 2017), ARIMA (Ariyo et al., [n. d.]), and GARCH (Hyup Roh, 2007). Later, deep learning methods like RNNs (Liu, 2018) and CNNs (Selvin et al., 2017; Durairaj and Mohan, 2022) enhanced nonlinear modeling capabilities. More recently, transformer-based models, such as Informer (Zhou et al., 2021) and FedFormer (Zhou et al., 2022), improved long-range dependency modeling for time series data. However, these models tend to be “case-specific,” requiring task-specific training. In contrast, the lastest pre-trained models for time-series data, like MOMENT (Goswami et al., 2024), Timer (Liu et al., 2024b), and TOKEN (Talukder et al., 2024), offer more generalized and adaptable solutions for time-series tasks.\nThe third line of research adopts multi-modality approaches, combining diverse data types to improve forecasting accuracy. Some studies incorporate text and audio (Qin and Yang, 2019; Yang et al., 2020) but often overlook time-series dependencies. Recent work has integrated time-series and textual data; for example, (Sawhney et al., 2020b; Sawhney et al., 2020a) employed SVM and GRU models to capture time-series features. However, these models are relatively shallow for extracting complex patterns. More recent studies (Lee et al., 2024; Jia et al., 2024) leverage transformer-based models for time-series analysis, better capturing deeper temporal structures. Building on these advancements, this paper aims to utilize state-of-the-art pre-trained models with enhanced feature fusion and causal learning for multi-modality forecasting.\n2.2. Salient Macroeconomic Factors\nWhich macroeconomic announcements have a greater impact on financial markets than others? This question has been widely studied in the financial literature, with Central Bank Communications standing out as the most-researched factor (CIESLAK et al., 2019; Gertler and Horvath, 2018; Masciandaro et al., 2024; Rosa, 2016; Tadle, 2022; Rosa, 2013; LUCCA and MOENCH, 2015; Rosa, 2011). Beyond central bank communications, various other macroeconomic factors have also been identified as significant drivers of market movements. Among these, Non-farm Payrolls, Unemployment Releases, Initial Unemployment Claims, ISM Manufacturing Index, GDP Advance Releases, Consumer Confidence Index, and Producer Price Index (PPI) Reports have been found to notably influence price movements and market volatility through empirical statistical testings (Pearce and Roley, 1984; Gilbert et al., 2010; Gilbert et al., 2017; Bartolini et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2004; Goldberg and Grisse, 2013). In this paper, we aim to leaverage the most significant factors evidented by the past financial literautre (Pearce and Roley, 1984; Gilbert et al., 2010; Gilbert et al., 2017; Bartolini et al., 2008; Kim et al., 2004; Goldberg and Grisse, 2013), which include FOMC Meeting Documents, Non-farm Payrolls, Unemployment Releases, Initial Unemployment Claims, ISM Manufacturing Index, GDP Advance Releases, Consumer Confidence Index, and Producer Price Index (PPI) Reports.\n2.3. Counterfactual Data Augmentation by LLMs\nCounterfactual Data Augmentation seeks to reduce spurious correlations and enhance model robustness. Kaushik et al. (2020) introduced a method that augments training data with counterfactuals written by human annotators, effectively helping to mitigate spurious patterns. Wu et al. (2021); Ross et al. (2022) later proposed the use of hand-crafted templates and trained text generators to create counterfactual data through predefined perturbation types. However, these methods are limited by their reliance on fixed perturbations. More recently, Chen et al. (2023); Wang et al. (2023) proposed more flexible, LLM-based approaches that leverage specifically designed in-context learning prompts and generation pipelines for counterfactual and instruction data generation. Following this direction, we present a counterfactual generation framework specifically designed for macroeconomic releases.\nTable 1.
