id=\"S2.SS1.p3\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS1.p3.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">In addition to our own volume, we introduce the instantaneous market volume process <math id=\"S2.SS1.p3.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"(V_{t})_{t}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">(V_{t})_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, assumed to be progressively measurable and nonnegative. The cumulated volume from 0 up to time <math id=\"S2.SS1.p3.m2\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"t\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">t</annotation></semantics></math> is denoted <math id=\"S2.SS1.p3.m3\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"Q_{t}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">Q_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>.<span id=\"footnote7\" class=\"ltx_note ltx_role_footnote\"><sup class=\"ltx_note_mark\">7</sup><span class=\"ltx_note_outer\"><span class=\"ltx_note_content\"><sup class=\"ltx_note_mark\">7</sup>\n              <span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_note\">7</span>\n              \n              \n            In other words, <math id=\"footnote7.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"Q_{t}=\\int_{0}^{t}V_{s}ds\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo rspace=\"0.111em\">=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace=\"0em\">𝑑</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">Q_{t}=\\int_{0}^{t}V_{s}ds</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></span></span></p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS1.p4\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS1.p4.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The price process of the stock is defined as a Brownian motion<span id=\"footnote8\" class=\"ltx_note ltx_role_footnote\"><sup class=\"ltx_note_mark\">8</sup><span class=\"ltx_note_outer\"><span class=\"ltx_note_content\"><sup class=\"ltx_note_mark\">8</sup>\n              <span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_note\">8</span>\n              \n              \n            The volatility parameter is not constrained to be a constant. It can be a deterministic function.</span></span></span> with a drift to account for market impact. Permanent market impact<span id=\"footnote9\" class=\"ltx_note ltx_role_footnote\"><sup class=\"ltx_note_mark\">9</sup><span class=\"ltx_note_outer\"><span class=\"ltx_note_content\"><sup class=\"ltx_note_mark\">9</sup>\n              <span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_note\">9</span>\n              \n              \n            Our model generalizes the linear model used in most optimal liquidation papers following Almgren and Chriss. It permits to account for the commonly observed nonlinearity of market impact. As shown in <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib16\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">16</a>]</cite>, we emphasize that there is no profitable (on average) round trip in our framework. Also, permanent market impact only depends on the initial and final positions and not on the trajectory.</span></span></span> is modeled by a function <math id=\"S2.SS1.p4.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"f:\\mathbb{R}^{*}_{+}\\rightarrow\\mathbb{R}_{+}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace=\"0.278em\" encoding=\"application/x-tex\">f:\\mathbb{R}^{*}_{+}\\rightarrow\\mathbb{R}_{+}</annotation></semantics></math>, assumed to be nonincreasing and integrable in <math id=\"S2.SS1.p4.m2\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"0\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">0</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>\n<table id=\"S2.Ex3\" Here, we choose to consider an expected utility framework with a CARA utility function. This framework boils down to a mean variance setting in the case of gaussian risks. ltx_font_bold\">.</span></h6>\n<div id=\"Pt0.ThmRemark2.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"Pt0.ThmRemark2.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"Pt0.ThmRemark2.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_italic\">The above definition of the VWAP can also be formulated as:</span></p>\n<table id=\"S2.Ex6\" class=\"ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table\">\n\n<tbody><tr class=\"ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline\">\n<td class=\"ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft\"></td>\n<td class=\"ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center\"><math id=\"S2.Ex6.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\text{VWAP}_{T}=\\int_{0}^{T}S_{t}dx_{t},\" display=\"block\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mtext class=\"ltx_mathvariant_italic\">VWAP</mtext><mi>T</mi></msub><mo rspace=\"0.111em\">=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation id=\"Pt0.ThmRemark2.p1.2\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"Pt0.ThmRemark2.p1.2.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_italic\">where <math id=\"Pt0.ThmRemark2.p1.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"x_{t}:=\\frac{Q_{t}}{Q_{T}}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>:=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">x_{t}:=\\frac{Q_{t}}{Q_{T}}</annotation></semantics></math>. This formulation is often used in the literature but it has an important drawback as the above integral is not <math id=\"Pt0.ThmRemark2.p1.m2\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\mathbb{F}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>𝔽</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathbb{F}</annotation></semantics></math>-adapted. Its natural filtration is indeed <math id=\"Pt0.ThmRemark2.p1.m3\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"(\\mathcal{G}_{t})_{t}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><msub><mi class=\"ltx_font_mathcaligraphic\">𝒢</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">(\\mathcal{G}_{t})_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> where:</span></p>\n<table id=\"S2.Ex7\" class=\"ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table\">\n\n<tbody><tr class=\"ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline\">\n<td class=\"ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft\"></td>\n<td class=\"ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center\"><math id=\"S2.Ex7.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\mathcal{G}_{t}:=\\mathcal{F}_{t}\\vee\\sigma(Q_{T}).\" display=\"block\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class=\"ltx_font_mathcaligraphic\">𝒢</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>:=</mo><mrow><msub><mi class=\"ltx_font_mathcaligraphic\">ℱ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∨</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace=\"0em\">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathcal{G}_{t}:=\\mathcal{F}_{t}\\vee\\sigma(Q_{T}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>\n<td class=\"ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright\"></td></tr></tbody>\n</table>\n</div>\n</div>\n<div id=\"Pt0.ThmRemark3\" class=\"ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_Remark\">\n<h6 class=\"ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem\"><span id=\"Pt0.ThmRemark3.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Remark 2.3</span></span><span id=\"Pt0.ThmRemark3.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">.</span></h6>\n<div id=\"Pt0.ThmRemark3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"Pt0.ThmRemark3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"Pt0.ThmRemark3.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_italic\">In the above definition of <math id=\"Pt0.ThmRemark3.p1.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"VWAP_{T}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mi>W</mi><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mi>A</mi><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">VWAP_{T}</annotation></semantics></math>, we did not include our own volume. An alternative definition, including our trades, is</span></p>\n<table id=\"S2.Ex8\" class=\"ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table\">\n\n<tbody><tr class=\"ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline\">\n<td class=\"ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft\"></td>\n<td class=\"ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center\"><math id=\"S2.Ex8.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\text{VWAP}^{\\prime}_{T}:=\\frac{\\int_{0}^{T}S_{t}(V_{t}+v_{t})dt}{Q_{T}+q_{0}}.\" display=\"block\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mtext class=\"ltx_mathvariant_italic\">VWAP</mtext><mi>T</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo>:=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace=\"0em\">𝑑</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace=\"0em\">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\text{VWAP}^{\\prime}_{T}:=\\frac{\\int_{0}^{T}S_{t}(V_{t}+v_{t})dt}{Q_{T}+q_{0}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>\n<td class=\"ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright\"></td></tr></tbody>\n</table>\n<p id=\"Pt0.ThmRemark3.p1.2\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"Pt0.ThmRemark3.p1.2.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_italic\">We shall see in the appendix of this article that the results we obtain with our simpler definition can be easily modified to be true in the case of the alternative definition.</span></p>\n</div>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS1.p9\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S2.SS1.p9.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The rationale for our optimization criterion (<a href=\"#S2.E1\" title=\"In 2.1 Setup and notations ‣ 2 General framework ‣ VWAP execution and guaranteed VWAP\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">2.1</span></a>) is the following. We consider a stock trader or an asset manager who wants to sell <math id=\"S2.SS1.p9.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"q_{0}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">q_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> shares at the VWAP over the period <math id=\"S2.SS1.p9.m2\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"[0,T]\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">[0,T]</annotation></semantics></math>. For that purpose, he signs with an intermediary (typically a broker) a guaranteed VWAP contract.<span id=\"footnote11\" class=\"ltx_note ltx_role_footnote\"><sup class=\"ltx_note_mark\">11</sup><span class=\"ltx_note_outer\"><span class=\"ltx_note_content\"><sup class=\"ltx_note_mark\">11</sup>\n              <span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_note\">11</span>\n              \n              \n            This is not an agency VWAP since, here, the VWAP is guaranteed (although its value is not known <em id=\"footnote11.1\" class=\"ltx_emph ltx_font_italic\">ex ante</em>).</span></span></span> He gives the intermediary its <math id=\"S2.SS1.p9.m3\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"q_{0}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">q_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> shares at time 0 and he receives at time <math id=\"S2.SS1.p9.m4\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"T\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">T</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id=\"S2.SS1.p9.m5\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"q_{0}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">q_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> times the VWAP computed over the period <math id=\"S2.SS1.p9.m6\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"[0,T]\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">[0,T]</annotation></semantics></math>, minus a premium – hereafter denoted <math id=\"S2.SS1.p9.m7\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\pi(q_{0})\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\pi(q_{0})</annotation></semantics></math> – to compensate the intermediary for the service and the associated costs, this premium being agreed upon at time <math id=\"S2.SS1.p9.m8\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"0\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">0</annotation></semantics></math>. The problem we address is the problem of the intermediary: he receives <math id=\"S2.SS1.p9.m9\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"q_{0}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">q_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> shares and sells them over the period <math id=\"S2.SS1.p9.m10\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"[0,T]\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">[0,T]</annotation></semantics></math> to obtain <math id=\"S2.SS1.p9.m11\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"X_{T}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">X_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> on its cash account at time <math id=\"S2.SS1.p9.m12\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"T\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">T</annotation></semantics></math>. Then, he gives his client <math id=\"S2.SS1.p9.m13\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"q_{0}\\text{VWAP}_{T}-\\pi(q_{0})\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><msub><mtext>VWAP</mtext><mi>T</mi></msub></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">q_{0}\\text{VWAP}_{T}-\\pi(q_{0})</annotation></semantics></math> in cash. Therefore, if the intermediary has a constant absolute risk aversion <math id=\"S2.SS1.p9.m14\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\gamma\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\gamma</annotation></semantics></math>, his liquidation strategy is obtained by maximizing</p>\n<table id=\"S2.Ex9\" class=\"ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table\">\n\n<tbody><tr class=\"ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline\">\n<td class=\"ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft\"></td>\n<td class=\"ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center\"><math id=\"S2.Ex9.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\mathbb{E}\\left[-\\exp\\left(-\\gamma(X_{T}-q_{0}\\text{VWAP}_{T}+\\pi(q_{0}))\\right)\\right]=\\exp(-\\gamma\\pi(q_{0}))\\mathbb{E}\\left[-\\exp\\left(-\\gamma(X_{T}-q_{0}\\text{VWAP}_{T})\\right)\\right].\" compute the reservation price of the intermediary, that is the price at which the intermediary is indifferent between accepting the contract and refusing it. This approach for pricing, also called indifference pricing, leads to the following definition for the premium of a guaranteed VWAP:<span id=\"footnote12\" class=\"ltx_note ltx_role_footnote\"><sup class=\"ltx_note_mark\">12</sup><span class=\"ltx_note_outer\"><span class=\"ltx_note_content\"><sup class=\"ltx_note_mark\">12</sup>\n              <span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_note\">12</span>\n              \n              \n            The premium in percentage is then <math id=\"footnote12.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\frac{\\pi(q_{0})}{q_{0}S_{0}}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mfrac><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\frac{\\pi(q_{0})}{q_{0}S_{0}}</annotation></semantics></math>. However, this is expressed in percentage of the initial price. In practice, some guaranteed VWAP contracts are also priced in basis points of the realized VWAP. We refer to Appendix B for this different definition of the premium and its consequences on our approach. Numerically, the two approaches provide similar figures in basis point of their respective reference price.</span></span></span></p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S2.SS1.p12\" class=\"ltx_para id=\"Pt0.ThmTheorem1.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_italic\">There exists a unique minimizer <math id=\"Pt0.ThmTheorem1.p1.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"q^{*}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><msup><mi>q</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">q^{*}</annotation></semantics></math> of <math id=\"Pt0.ThmTheorem1.p1.m2\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace=\"0em\" Moreover we have that <math id=\"Pt0.ThmTheorem1.p1.m4\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"q^{*}(t)\\leq q_{0}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>q</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≤</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">q^{*}(t)\\leq q_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> for all <math id=\"Pt0.ThmTheorem1.p1.m5\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"t\\in[0,T]\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">[</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">t\\in[0,T]</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></p>\n</div>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S3.p12\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S3.p12.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S3.p12.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Proof:\n<br class=\"ltx_break\"></span></p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S3.p13\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S3.p13.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">We divide the proof in three steps.\n<br class=\"ltx_break\"></p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S3.p14\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S3.p14.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"S3.p14.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_italic\">Step 1:</span> We first show that any strategy can be improved by considering a new one taking values in <math id=\"S3.p14.m1\" class=\"ltx_math_unparsed\" alttext=\"(-\\infty,q_{0}]\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mo lspace=\"0em\">−</mo><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">∞</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">(-\\infty,q_{0}]</annotation></semantics></math>. Indeed for <math id=\"S3.p14.m2\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"q\\in AC_{q_{0},0}(0,T)\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">q\\in AC_{q_{0},0}(0,T)</annotation></semantics></math>, we define <math id=\"S3.p14.m3\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\tilde{q}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mover accent=\"true\"><mi>q</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\tilde{q}</annotation></semantics></math> by <math id=\"S3.p14.m4\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\tilde{q}(t):=\\min(q_{0},q(t))\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent=\"true\"><mi>q</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mi>min</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\tilde{q}(t):=\\min(q_{0},q(t))</annotation></semantics></math>. We have <math id=\"S3.p14.m5\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\tilde{q}\\in AC_{q_{0},0}(0,T)\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mover accent=\"true\"><mi>q</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\tilde{q}\\in AC_{q_{0},0}(0,T)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id=\"S3.p14.m6\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\dot{\\tilde{q}}(t)=\\dot{q}(t){\\bf{1}}_{q(t)&lt;q_{0}}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent=\"true\"><mover accent=\"true\"><mi>q</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mo>˙</mo></mover><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mover accent=\"true\"><mi>q</mi><mo>˙</mo></mover><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><msub><mn>𝟏</mn><mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\dot{\\tilde{q}}(t)=\\dot{q}(t){\\bf{1}}_{q(t)&lt;q_{0}}</annotation></semantics></math>. Therefore, since <math id=\"S3.p14.m7\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"L\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">L</annotation></semantics></math> is even and increasing on <math id=\"S3.p14.m8\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\mathbb{R}_{+}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><msub><mi>ℝ</mi><mo>+</mo></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathbb{R}_{+}</annotation></semantics></math>, we have:</p>\n<table id=\"S3.Ex15\" id=\"S3.p14.3\" class=\"ltx_p\">Eventually, we have that</p>\n<table id=\"S3.Ex17\" class=\"ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table\">\n\n<tbody><tr class=\"ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline\">\n<td then show the uniqueness of the minimizer. Let us consider <math id=\"S3.p15.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"q_{1}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">q_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id=\"S3.p15.m2\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"q_{2}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">q_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> two minimizers of <math id=\"S3.p15.m3\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\mathcal{I}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi class=\"ltx_font_mathcaligraphic\">ℐ</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\mathcal{I}</annotation></semantics></math> such that <math id=\"S3.p15.m4\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"q_{1}\\neq q_{2}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>≠</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">q_{1}\\neq q_{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. We know, using Step 1, that <math id=\"S3.p15.m5\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"q_{1}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">q_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id=\"S3.p15.m6\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"q_{2}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">q_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> take values in <math id=\"S3.p15.m7\" class=\"ltx_math_unparsed\" alttext=\"(-\\infty,q_{0}]\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mo lspace=\"0em\">−</mo><mi mathvariant=\"normal\">∞</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">(-\\infty,q_{0}]</annotation></semantics></math>. We next define <math id=\"S3.p15.m8\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"q\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">q</annotation></semantics></math> by <math id=\"S3.p15.m9\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"q(t):=\\frac{q_{1}(t)+q_{2}(t)}{2}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">q(t):=\\frac{q_{1}(t)+q_{2}(t)}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. In that case indeed, we have that the optimal strategy is to follow the market volume curve. lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">-\\frac{q_{0}}{Q_{T}}=H^{\\prime}(p(t))</annotation></semantics></math> so that:</p>\n<table id=\"S4.Ex3\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo alttext=\"\\dot{p}(t)=0=\\gamma\\sigma^{2}\\left(q(t)-q_{0}\\left(1-\\frac{Q_{t}}{Q_{T}}\\right)\\right)\" display=\"block\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent=\"true\"><mi>p</mi><mo>˙</mo></mover><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><msup><mi>σ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace=\"0em\" ltx_eqn_center_padright\"></td></tr></tbody>\n</table>\n<p id=\"S4.SS1.p3.3\" class=\"ltx_p\">This proves that <math id=\"S4.SS1.p3.m7\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"q=q^{*}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>q</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">q=q^{*}</annotation></semantics></math>, hence the first part of the result.\n<br class=\"ltx_break\"></p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S4.SS1.p4\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS1.p4.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Coming to the premium, we have:</p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S4.SS1.p5\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<table id=\"S4.Ex5\" class=\"ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table\">\n\n<tbody><tr class=\"ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline\">\n<td class=\"ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft\"></td>\n<td class=\"ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center\"><math id=\"S4.Ex5.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\pi(q_{0})=\\int_{0}^{q_{0}}F(z)dz+\\mathcal{I}(q^{*})=\\int_{0}^{T}V_{t}L\\left(-\\frac{q_{0}}{Q_{T}}\\right)dt=Q_{T}L\\left(\\frac{q_{0}}{Q_{T}}\\right).\" display=\"block\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace=\"0.111em\">=</mo><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></msubsup><mrow><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace=\"0em\">𝑑</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi class=\"ltx_font_mathcaligraphic\">ℐ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><msup><mi>q</mi><mo>∗</mo></msup><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace=\"0.111em\">=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mi>L</mi><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mo lspace=\"0em\">−</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace=\"0em\">𝑑</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mi>L</mi><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></mfrac><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace=\"0em\">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\pi(q_{0})=\\int_{0}^{q_{0}}F(z)dz+\\mathcal{I}(q^{*})=\\int_{0}^{T}V_{t}L\\left(-\\frac{q_{0}}{Q_{T}}\\right)dt=Q_{T}L\\left(\\frac{q_{0}}{Q_{T}}\\right).</annotation></semantics></math></td>\n<td class=\"ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright\"></td></tr></tbody>\n</table>\n<p id=\"S4.SS1.p5.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">∎\n<br class=\"ltx_break\"></p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S4.SS1.p6\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS1.p6.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The result of the above Proposition deserves a few comments. It states that, in the absence of permanent market impact, the optimal strategy is to have a trading curve that has the same shape as the relative market volume curve. One consequence is that, in practice, as far as the trading strategy is concerned, when permanent market impact can be (or is) ignored, one is interested in the estimation of the relative market volume curve and not in the estimation of the absolute value of the market volume. This remark is particularly important to understand why the deterministic market volume assumption provides a rather acceptable approximation of the real case for VWAP trading. Although the total volume traded over a day is highly variable, we know that the relative market volume curve is stable from one day to the other (except on witching days). Since the cumulated volume <math id=\"S4.SS1.p6.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"Q_{T}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">Q_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> only appears in the execution strategy through the ratio <math id=\"S4.SS1.p6.m2\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\frac{Q_{t}}{Q_{T}}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mfrac><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></mfrac><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\frac{Q_{t}}{Q_{T}}</annotation></semantics></math>, considering it stochastic does not play any role if we have already assumed that the relative market volume curve is deterministic.<span id=\"footnote13\" class=\"ltx_note ltx_role_footnote\"><sup class=\"ltx_note_mark\">13</sup><span class=\"ltx_note_outer\"><span class=\"ltx_note_content\"><sup class=\"ltx_note_mark\">13</sup>\n              <span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_note\">13</span>\n              \n              \n            In practice, most institutions use relative market volume curves computed in advance, based on historical data.</span></span></span> The value of <math id=\"S4.SS1.p6.m3\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"Q_{T}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">Q_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> is however important to determine the premium of the guaranteed VWAP contract. Since this premium must be decided upon at time <math id=\"S4.SS1.p6.m4\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"t=0\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">t=0</annotation></semantics></math>, the value of <math id=\"S4.SS1.p6.m5\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"Q_{T}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">Q_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> must be understood<span id=\"footnote14\" class=\"ltx_note ltx_role_footnote\"><sup class=\"ltx_note_mark\">14</sup><span class=\"ltx_note_outer\"><span class=\"ltx_note_content\"><sup class=\"ltx_note_mark\">14</sup>\n              <span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_note\">14</span>\n              \n              \n            We ignore here part of the risk.</span></span></span> as a forecast at time <math id=\"S4.SS1.p6.m6\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"0\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">0</annotation></semantics></math> of the total market volume over the period <math id=\"S4.SS1.p6.m7\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"[0,T]\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">[0,T]</annotation></semantics></math>.\n<br class=\"ltx_break\"></p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S4.SS1.p7\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS1.p7.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">The above remarks only apply in the absence of permanent market impact but the assumption of a deterministic market volume is acceptable if we deviate slightly through the introduction of a small permanent market impact. Now, our goal is to understand the influence of permanent market impact in this framework, and the nature of the related deviation of the optimal strategy from the relative market volume curve.\n<br class=\"ltx_break\"></p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S4.SS2\" class=\"ltx_subsection\">\n<h3 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_subsection\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection\">4.2 </span>VWAP strategies when <math id=\"S4.SS2.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"V_{t}=V\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>V</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">V_{t}=V</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id=\"S4.SS2.m2\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"f=k\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">f=k</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id=\"S4.SS2.m3\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"L(\\rho)=\\eta\\rho^{2}\" display=\"inline\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS2.p17.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">This result permits to understand the role played by permanent market impact. We indeed have that <math id=\"S4.SS2.p17.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"w\\geq 0\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">w\\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math> and therefore that the liquidation must occur more rapidly with the addition of permanent market impact. The rationale underlying this point is that the intermediary is going to pay <math id=\"S4.SS2.p17.m2\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"q_{0}\\text{VWAP}_{T}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><msub><mtext>VWAP</mtext><mi>T</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">q_{0}\\text{VWAP}_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> to the client and therefore he has an incentive to sell rapidly so that the price moves down, resulting in a lower VWAP. If <math id=\"S4.SS2.p17.m3\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"k\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">k</annotation></semantics></math> is large, the optimal strategy may even be to oversell before buying back the shares so as to reduce the value of the VWAP (see below).\n<br class=\"ltx_break\"></p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S4.SS2.p18\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS2.p18.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Coming to the premium for a guaranteed VWAP, it is straightforward to see that if <math id=\"S4.SS2.p18.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"q(t)=q_{0}\\left(1-\\frac{t}{T}\\right)\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mi>t</mi><mi>T</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">q(t)=q_{0}\\left(1-\\frac{t}{T}\\right)</annotation></semantics></math> the premium would be equal to <math id=\"S4.SS2.p18.m2\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\frac{\\eta}{VT}q_{0}^{2}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>η</mi><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\frac{\\eta}{VT}q_{0}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>. The dashed line corresponds to <math id=\"S4.F1.m20\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"q_{0}\\left(1-\\frac{t}{T}\\right)\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mi>t</mi><mi>T</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">q_{0}\\left(1-\\frac{t}{T}\\right)</annotation></semantics></math>.</figcaption>\n</figure>\n<div id=\"S4.SS2.p23\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS2.p23.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">It is important to understand what is at play here. An agent willing to sell shares at a price close to the VWAP over a given period has usually two possibilities. He may call his favorite broker and ask for an agency VWAP order. In that case, the broker will try to sell shares as close as possible to the VWAP and the price obtained will be the price for the agent. In other words, the risk is borne by the agent. The other possibility is to enter a guaranteed VWAP contract. In that case, the price obtained by the agent will always be the VWAP. Our point is that the VWAP obtained by the agent in a guaranteed VWAP contract is not the same as the VWAP obtained on average through agency trades. In a guaranteed VWAP contract, the counterpart has indeed an incentive to sell more rapidly in order to push down the price and hence push down the VWAP. This is not market price manipulation, as the overall impact of the execution process would be the same independently of the trajectory. This is however a form of VWAP manipulation. Is the agent harmed? Somehow yes, although he gets its benchmark price. Nonetheless, since the counterpart of the contract makes money by selling more rapidly at the beginning of the execution process, he can redistribute part of it through a reduction of the premium…\n<br class=\"ltx_break\"></p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S4.SS2.p24\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S4.SS2.p24.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">To measure the difference between the naive strategy <math id=\"S4.SS2.p24.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"q^{naive}(t)=q_{0}\\left(1-\\frac{t}{T}\\right)\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>q</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mi>v</mi><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mi>e</mi></mrow></msup><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mi>t</mi><mi>T</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">q^{naive}(t)=q_{0}\\left(1-\\frac{t}{T}\\right)</annotation></semantics></math> and the optimal strategy, the best indicator is the premium of a guaranteed VWAP contract <math id=\"S4.SS2.p24.m2\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\pi(q_{0})\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mi>π</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\pi(q_{0})</annotation></semantics></math>. intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">S_{0}=50</annotation></semantics></math>, <math form formulas could be obtained. In general, this is not the case and we present here a general method to approximate the solution of the Hamiltonian system. It is important to notice that the use of the Hamiltonian system is preferable to the use of Euler-Lagrange equation when it comes to numerics since the problem remains of order 1. The method we use to approximate the solution <math id=\"S4.SS3.p1.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"(p,q)\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mo The dashed line corresponds to <math id=\"S4.F3.m26\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"q_{0}\\left(1-\\frac{t}{T}\\right)\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mfrac><mi>t</mi><mi>T</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">q_{0}\\left(1-\\frac{t}{T}\\right)</annotation></semantics></math>.</figcaption>\n</figure>\n</section>\n</section>\n<section id=\"S5\" class=\"ltx_section\">\n<h2 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_section\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_section\">5 </span>Going beyond the deterministic case</h2>\n\n<div id=\"S5.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S5.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">In the previous sections of this article, we focused on the case of a deterministic volume curve. The reason for this is twofold. Firstly, it permits to understand the role played by permanent market impact in a tractable case. Secondly, it corresponds to the way VWAP strategies are often built in practice and we explained above why it was a good approximation. Practitioners usually compute relative market volume curves based on historical data and try to follow this curve to get a price as close as possible to the VWAP.<span id=\"footnote15\" class=\"ltx_note ltx_role_footnote\"><sup class=\"ltx_note_mark\">15</sup><span class=\"ltx_note_outer\"><span class=\"ltx_note_content\"><sup class=\"ltx_note_mark\">15</sup>\n            <span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_note\">15</span>\n            \n            \n          In practice, there are specific relative volume curves on special (witching) days. Some advanced desks also use several deterministic curves and may switch from one regime to another.</span></span></span>\n<br class=\"ltx_break\"></p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S5.p2\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S5.p2.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">We now briefly explore the case of stochastic market volume. The aim of this section is to provide a Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman PDE to characterize the optimal liquidation strategy (that is no longer deterministic, and hence no longer a trading curve decided upon in advance, at time <math id=\"S5.p2.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"0\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">0</annotation></semantics></math>) and the premium of a guaranteed VWAP contract. A similar approach, using stochastic optimal control, was adopted by Frei and Westray <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib12\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">12</a>]</cite> in the mean-variance setup. However, in their paper, the initial filtration is augmented with the knowledge of the final volume and this makes their approach questionable for practical use.\n<br class=\"ltx_break\"></p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S5.p3\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S5.p3.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">In the model we consider, the instantaneous market volume is modeled by a simple stochastic process but it can be generalized to other processes. In fact, our main goal is to write the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman PDE characterizing the solution of our problem using as few variables as possible. If one considers indeed our problem with stochastic market volume in its initial form, 7 variables are necessary to describe the problem: the time <math id=\"S5.p3.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"t\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">t</annotation></semantics></math>, the trader’s inventory <math id=\"S5.p3.m2\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"q\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">q</annotation></semantics></math>, the asset market price <math id=\"S5.p3.m3\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"S\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">S</annotation></semantics></math>, the cash account <math id=\"S5.p3.m4\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"X\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">X</annotation></semantics></math>, the instantaneous market volume <math id=\"S5.p3.m5\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"V\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">V</annotation></semantics></math>, the cumulated market volume <math id=\"S5.p3.m6\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"Q\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>Q</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">Q</annotation></semantics></math>, and a variable linked to the VWAP, namely <math id=\"S5.p3.m7\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\int_{0}^{t}V_{s}S_{s}ds\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mi>t</mi></msubsup><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mrow><mo rspace=\"0em\">𝑑</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\int_{0}^{t}V_{s}S_{s}ds</annotation></semantics></math>. Using two changes of variables, we manage to restrict the number of variables to 5. Classical numerical (PDE) methods may fail to approximate the solution of the PDE, but some probabilistic methods may be efficient (see <cite class=\"ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite\">[<a href=\"#bib.bib13\" title=\"\" class=\"ltx_ref\">13</a>]</cite> for robust methods in the case of problems in high dimension).\n<br class=\"ltx_break\"></p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S5.p4\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S5.p4.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">Coming to the model, we consider that the instantaneous volume is given by <math id=\"S5.p4.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"V_{t}=g(t)e^{\\alpha B_{t}-\\alpha^{2}t/2}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>α</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">V_{t}=g(t)e^{\\alpha B_{t}-\\alpha^{2}t/2}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id=\"S5.p4.m2\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"g\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>g</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">g</annotation></semantics></math> is <math id=\"S5.p4.m3\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"C^{1}(\\mathbb{R},\\mathbb{R}_{+}^{*})\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>C</mi><mn>1</mn></msup><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mi>ℝ</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>ℝ</mi><mo>+</mo><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">C^{1}(\\mathbb{R},\\mathbb{R}_{+}^{*})</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id=\"S5.p4.m4\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"B\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">B</annotation></semantics></math> is a Brownian motion independent of <math id=\"S5.p4.m5\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"W\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>W</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">W</annotation></semantics></math>, and where <math id=\"S5.p4.m6\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\alpha&gt;0\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\alpha&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>. The dynamics of <math id=\"S5.p4.m7\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"V\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">V</annotation></semantics></math> is then given by the stochastic differential equation:</p>\n<table id=\"S5.Ex1\" class=\"ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table\">\n\n<tbody><tr class=\"ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline\">\n<td class=\"ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft\"></td>\n<td class=\"ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center\"><math id=\"S5.Ex1.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\frac{dV_{t}}{V_{t}}=\\frac{g^{\\prime}(t)}{g(t)}dt+\\alpha dB_{t}.\" display=\"block\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>g</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace=\"0em\">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">\\frac{dV_{t}}{V_{t}}=\\frac{g^{\\prime}(t)}{g(t)}dt+\\alpha dB_{t}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>\n<td class=\"ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright\"></td></tr></tbody>\n</table>\n<p id=\"S5.p4.2\" class=\"ltx_p\"><math id=\"S5.p4.m8\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"g(t)\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy=\"false\">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy=\"false\">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">g(t)</annotation></semantics></math> represents obviously the instantaneous market volume, on average, at time <math id=\"S5.p4.m9\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"t\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">t</annotation></semantics></math>. In Europe, it is a W-shaped curve with a peak corresponding to the opening of the US market.\n<br class=\"ltx_break\"></p>\n</div>\n<div id=\"Pt0.ThmRemark1b\" class=\"ltx_theorem ltx_theorem_Remark\">\n<h6 class=\"ltx_title ltx_runin ltx_title_theorem\"><span class=\"ltx_tag ltx_tag_theorem\"><span id=\"Pt0.ThmRemark1b.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">Remark 5.1</span></span><span id=\"Pt0.ThmRemark1b.2\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_bold\">.</span></h6>\n<div id=\"Pt0.ThmRemark1b.p1\" class=\"ltx_para\">\n<p id=\"Pt0.ThmRemark1b.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\"><span id=\"Pt0.ThmRemark1b.p1.1.1\" class=\"ltx_text ltx_font_italic\">Other dynamics can be considered. The goal of this last section is not to consider the best possible model for volumes but rather to show how the complexity of the model can be reduced through changes of variables.\n<br class=\"ltx_break\"></span></p>\n</div>\n</div>\n<div id=\"S5.p5\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"S5.p5.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">In order to consider a non-degenerated problem (one may alternatively use the stochastic target framework), we consider a slightly modified problem where <math id=\"S5.p5.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"q_{T}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">q_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> is not forced to be equal to <math id=\"S5.p5.m2\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"0\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mn>0</mn><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">0</annotation></semantics></math>. Rather than imposing <math id=\"S5.p5.m3\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"q_{T}=0\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">q_{T}=0</annotation></semantics></math>, we consider that, at time <math id=\"S5.p5.m4\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"T\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">T</annotation></semantics></math>, the remaining stocks are not liquidated at price <math id=\"S5.p5.m5\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"S_{T}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">S_{T}</annotation></semantics></math> but rather at price <math id=\"S5.p5.m6\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"S_{T}-Kq_{T}\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mi>T</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo lspace=\"0em\" rspace=\"0em\">​</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>T</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">S_{T}-Kq_{T}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id=\"S5.p5.m7\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"K\" display=\"inline\" intent=\":literal\"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding=\"application/x-tex\">K</annotation></semantics></math> is chosen positive and high enough to discourage the trader to keep a large position <math id=\"S5.p5.m8\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"q_{T}\" display=\"inline\" ltx_title_section\">Conclusion</h2>\n\n<div id=\"Sx1.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"Sx1.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">In this article we built a model to find the optimal strategy to liquidate a portfolio in the case of a guaranteed VWAP contract. When there is permanent market impact, we showed that the best strategy is not to replicate the VWAP but rather to sell more rapidly to push down the VWAP. Also, we use the indifference pricing approach to give a price to guaranteed VWAP contracts and we showed that taking into account permanent market impact permits, at least theoretically, to reduce substantially the price of guaranteed VWAP contracts. Finally, in the case of stochastic volumes, we developed a new model with only 5 variables and not 7 variables as in a naive approach.\n<br class=\"ltx_break\"></p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"Sx2\" class=\"ltx_section\">\n<h2 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_section\">Appendix A: <math id=\"Sx2.m1\" class=\"ltx_Math\" alttext=\"\\text{VWAP}_{T}\" display=\"inline\" Hence, if our volume represents a few percent of the market volume, using one definition of VWAP or the other does not really make a difference. Also, when the market volume process is assumed to be deterministic, the simple model we used over the course of this article leads to results that can be used when our volume is taken into account, if we apply the right multiplicative factors.\n<br class=\"ltx_break\">In the case of stochastic volume, instead of changing the values of the volatility and the market impact, we adapt the dynamic problem (<a href=\"#S5.E2\" title=\"In 5 Going beyond the deterministic case ‣ VWAP execution and guaranteed VWAP\" class=\"ltx_ref\"><span class=\"ltx_text ltx_ref_tag\">5.2</span></a>) with the new adapted slippage, and we obtain the same PDE with a different terminal condition, which does not induce higher complexity.\n<br class=\"ltx_break\"></p>\n</div>\n</section>\n<section id=\"Sx3\" class=\"ltx_section\">\n<h2 class=\"ltx_title ltx_title_section\">Appendix B: Relative pricing of guaranteed VWAP contracts</h2>\n\n<div id=\"Sx3.p1\" class=\"ltx_para ltx_noindent\">\n<p id=\"Sx3.p1.1\" class=\"ltx_p\">We now explore, for a deterministic volume curve, the case where the guaranteed VWAP contract is priced in basis point of the VWAP.       "text": "[1306.2832] VWAP execution and guaranteed VWAP\nVWAP execution and guaranteed VWAPThanks: This research has been conducted with the support of the Research\nInitiative “Exécution optimale et statistiques de la liquidité haute\nfréquence” under the aegis of the Europlace Institute of Finance. The\nauthors would like to thank Chris Frey (University of Alberta), Nicolas Grandchamp des Raux (HSBC France),\nJean-Michel Lasry (University Paris-Dauphine), Charles-Albert Lehalle\n(CFM), Christopher Ulph (HSBC), Silviu Vlasceanu (Kepler-Cheuvreux) and Nicholas Westray (Deutsche Bank)\nfor the exchanges we had on the subject. Two anonymous referees also deserve to be thanked for their remarks that permitted to improve the paper in a significant manner.\nOlivier Guéant\nNote: Université Paris-Diderot, UFR de\nMathématiques, Laboratoire Jacques-Louis Lions, gueant@ljll.univ-paris-diderot.fr\nGuillaume Royer\nNote: CMAP, Ecole Polytechnique Paris, guillaume.royer@polytechnique.edu.\nAbstract\nOptimal liquidation using VWAP strategies has been considered in the literature, though never in the presence of permanent market impact and only rarely with execution costs. Moreover, only VWAP strategies have been studied and the pricing of guaranteed VWAP contracts has never been addressed. In this article, we develop a model to price guaranteed VWAP contracts in a general framework for market impact and we highlight the differences between an agency VWAP and a guaranteed VWAP contract. Numerical methods and applications are also provided.\nKey words: Optimal liquidation, VWAP strategy, Guaranteed VWAP contract, Optimal control, Indifference pricing\n1 Introduction\nTraders or asset managers willing to sell blocks of shares are increasingly using execution algorithms. Amongst the strategies proposed by brokers, the most widely studied from an academic point of view is the Implementation Shortfall (IS) strategy. The classical modeling framework for optimal liquidation, developed by Almgren and Chriss in their seminal papers [1, 2], is indeed focused on IS orders benchmarked on the arrival price, that is the price at the beginning of the liquidation process. In the case of IS orders, the agent faces a trade-off between selling slowly to reduce execution costs and selling rapidly to limit the influence of price fluctuations. Although almost all the literature on optimal liquidation deals with IS orders, IS algorithms usually account for less volume than VWAP (Volume Weighted Average Price) algorithms – see for instance [3, 20]. The aim of traders when they choose VWAP orders is to focus on the reduction of execution costs: the order is split into smaller ones and the associated transactions occur on a pre-determined period to obtain a price as close as possible to the average price over this period (weighted by market volume).11\n 1\n On the contrary, when an investor chooses an IS algorithm, the execution process is fast at the beginning in order to obtain a price close to the one at inception. Execution costs are then usually higher for an IS than for a VWAP algorithm. VWAP is also a neutral and rather fair benchmark to evaluate execution processes. Many agents are willing to trade as close as possible to the VWAP as they are benchmarked on the VWAP.\nAlthough VWAP orders represent a large part of algorithmic trading, there are only a few papers about VWAP orders in the academic literature. The first important paper regarding liquidation with VWAP benchmark was written by Konishi [19]. He developed a simple model and looked for the best static strategy, that is the best trading curve decided upon at the beginning of the liquidation process (his goal is to minimize the variance of the slippage with respect to the VWAP). He found that the optimal trading curve for VWAP liquidation has the same shape as the relative market volume curve when volatility and market volume are uncorrelated. He also quantified the deviation from the relative market volume curve in the correlated case. The model was then extended by McCulloch and Kazakov [22] with the addition of a drift in a more constrained framework. McCulloch and Kazakov also developed a dynamic model [23] in which they conditioned the optimal trajectory with perfect knowledge of the volume by the available information at each period of time. Bouchard and Dang proposed in [6] to use a stochastic target framework to develop VWAP algorithms. Recently, Carmona and Li [10] also developed a model for VWAP trading in which the trader can explicitly choose between market orders and limit orders to buy/sell shares.22\n 2\n Our approach, consistently with the usual understanding of the Almgren-Chriss approach, does not prevent the use of limit orders. An execution algorithm is usually made of two layers: a strategic layer, which controls the risk with respect to a\nbenchmark (here the VWAP), and a tactical layer, which seeks liquidity inside order books, through all types of orders, and across other (lit or dark) liquidity pools. Our model is only concerned with the strategic layer: we want to obtain a trading curve that will then be followed by the trader using limit orders, market orders, etc. Related to this literature on VWAP trading (see also [17, 18, 29]), an academic literature appeared on market volume models. The papers by Bialkowski et al. [4, 5] or McCulloch [21] are instances of such papers modeling market volume dynamics and the intraday seasonality of relative volume. However, all these papers ignore an important point: market impact. The only paper dealing with VWAP trading and involving a form of market impact is the interesting paper by Frei and Westray33\n 3\n This paper is particularly interesting since the authors characterize the unique way to model the volume process such that the relative market volume is independent from the total cumulated market volume. [12]. In this paper, the price obtained by the trader is not the market price but a price depending linearly44\n 4\n Their assumption of linearity for execution costs is an acceptable one, although evidence proves that it is rather sublinear. It permits to obtain closed-form solutions. on the desired volume (as in the early models of Almgren and Chriss). However, there is no permanent market impact in their model, while it plays an important role in our paper.\nThe aim of our model is to include permanent market impact (see [16] for the framework we use) and any form of execution costs in a model for VWAP liquidation. Also, our goal is not to obtain a price as close as possible to the VWAP but rather to understand how to provide a guaranteed VWAP service while mitigating risk. In other words, we want to find the optimal strategy if we are given a certain quantity of shares and asked to deliver the VWAP over a predefined period. In addition to the optimal strategy underlying a guaranteed VWAP contract, we are interested in the price of such a contract. For that purpose, we use indifference pricing55\n 5\n For a general review on indifference pricing, the interested reader may refer to [9]. in a CARA framework, as in [15] where the author prices a large block of shares. This price for a guaranteed VWAP contract is the minimum premium the trader needs to pay to the broker so that the latter accepts to deliver the VWAP to the former. It depends on the size of the order, on liquidity and market conditions, and on the risk aversion of the broker.\nIn Section 2, we present the general framework of our model. We introduce the definition of the VWAP and the forms of market impact used in the model. The optimization criterion is defined and the price/premium of a guaranteed VWAP contract is defined using indifference pricing. In Section 3, we characterize the optimal liquidation strategy when the market volume curve is assumed to be known (deterministic case), along with the premium of the guaranteed VWAP contract. In Section 4, we focus on special cases and numerics. We show that, in the absence of permanent market impact, the optimal trading curve has the same shape as the market volume curve. We consider also the case of linear permanent market impact and quadratic execution costs that permits to get closed form solutions and to better understand the role played by permanent market impact. Finally, an efficient numerical method is provided to approximate the solution in the general case. In the last section, we extend our model to the case of stochastic volumes and we characterize the price of a guaranteed VWAP with a PDE.\n2 General framework\n2.1 Setup and notations\nWe consider a filtered probability space (Ω,𝔽,(ℱt)t≥0,ℙ)\\left(\\Omega,\\mathbb{F},\\left(\\mathcal{F}_{t}\\right)_{t\\geq 0},\\mathbb{P}\\right) corresponding to the available information on the market, namely the market price and market volume of a stock up to the observation time. For T>0T>0, we denote 𝒫⁡(0,T)\\mathcal{P}(0,T) the set of ℝ\\mathbb{R}-valued progressively measurable processes on [0,T].\nWe consider a trader who wants to sell q0>0q_{0}>0 shares66\n 6\n A similar approach can be considered in the case of a buying order. over the time period [0,T][0,T]. His liquidation strategy during this period – hereafter denoted vv – is modeled as a stochastic process belonging to the admissible set\n𝒜:={v∈𝒫(0,T),∫0T|vt|dt∈L∞(Ω),∫0Tvtdt=q0,ℙ−a.s.}.\\mathcal{A}:=\\left\\{v\\in\\mathcal{P}(0,T),\\int_{0}^{T}|v_{t}|dt\\in L^{\\infty}(\\Omega),\\int_{0}^{T}v_{t}dt=q_{0},\\ \\mathbb{P}-\\text{a.s.}\\right\\}.\nTo model the trader’s portfolio, we introduce a process (qt)t(q_{t})_{t} that gives the number of shares remaining in the portfolio at time tt:\nqt=q0−∫0tvs​𝑑s.q_{t}=q_{0}-\\int_{0}^{t}v_{s}ds.\nIn addition to our own volume, we introduce the instantaneous market volume process (Vt)t(V_{t})_{t}, assumed to be progressively measurable and nonnegative. The cumulated volume from 0 up to time tt is denoted QtQ_{t}.77\n 7\n In other words, Qt=∫0tVs​𝑑sQ_{t}=\\int_{0}^{t}V_{s}ds.\nThe price process of the stock is defined as a Brownian motion88\n 8\n The volatility parameter is not constrained to be a constant. It can be a deterministic function. with a drift to account for market impact. Permanent market impact99\n 9\n Our model generalizes the linear model used in most optimal liquidation papers following Almgren and Chriss. It permits to account for the commonly observed nonlinearity of market impact. As shown in [16], we emphasize that there is no profitable (on average) round trip in our framework. Also, permanent market impact only depends on the initial and final positions and not on the trajectory. is modeled by a function f:ℝ+∗→ℝ+f:\\mathbb{R}^{*}_{+}\\rightarrow\\mathbb{R}_{+}, assumed to be nonincreasing and integrable in 00:\nd​St=σ​d​Wt−f⁡(|q0−qt|)​vt​d​t,σ>0.dS_{t}=\\sigma dW_{t}-f\\left(\\left|q_{0}-q_{t}\\right|\\right)v_{t}dt,\\ \\ \\sigma>0.\nThe price received by the trader at time tt is not StS_{t} because of temporary market impact. This temporary market impact, also referred to as execution costs, is modeled through the introduction of a function L∈C⁡(ℝ,ℝ+)L\\in C(\\mathbb{R},\\mathbb{R}_{+}) verifying:\n• \nL⁡(0)=0L(0)=0,\n• \nLL is an even function,\n• \nLL is increasing on ℝ+\\mathbb{R}_{+},\n• \nLL is strictly convex,\n• \nLL is asymptotically superlinear, that is:\nlimρ→+∞L⁡(ρ)ρ=+∞.\\lim_{\\rho\\to+\\infty}\\frac{L(\\rho)}{\\rho}=+\\infty.\nRemark 2.1.\nIn applications, LL is often a power function, i.e. L⁡(ρ)=η​|ρ|1+ϕL(\\rho)=\\eta\\left|\\rho\\right|^{1+\\phi} with ϕ>0\\phi>0, or a function of the form L⁡(ρ)=η​|ρ|1+ϕ+ψ​|ρ|L(\\rho)=\\eta\\left|\\rho\\right|^{1+\\phi}+\\psi|\\rho| with ϕ,ψ>0\\phi,\\psi>0.\nFor any v∈𝒜v\\in\\mathcal{A}, we define the cash process XvX^{v} (hereafter denoted XX to simplify notations) by:\nXt=Xtv=∫0t(vs​Ss−Vs​L​(vsVs))​𝑑s.X_{t}=X_{t}^{v}=\\int_{0}^{t}\\left(v_{s}S_{s}-V_{s}L\\left(\\frac{v_{s}}{V_{s}}\\right)\\right)ds.\nWe are interested in the following optimization problem:\nsupv∈𝒜𝔼⁡[−exp⁡(−γ⁡(XT−q0​VWAPT))],\\displaystyle\\sup_{v\\in\\mathcal{A}}\\mathbb{E}\\left[-\\exp\\left(-\\gamma(X_{T}-q_{0}\\text{VWAP}_{T})\\right)\\right],\n(2.1)\nwhere1010\n 10\n The limiting case γ=0\\gamma=0 corresponds to risk neutrality. Here, we choose to consider an expected utility framework with a CARA utility function. This framework boils down to a mean variance setting in the case of gaussian risks. Considering a utility function is more rigorous from an economic viewpoint, especially when it comes to pricing. γ>0\\gamma>0 is the absolute risk aversion parameter, and where VWAPT\\text{VWAP}_{T} stands for the volume weighted average price (VWAP) on the period [0,T][0,T], i.e.:\nVWAPT:=∫0TSt​Vt​𝑑t∫0TVt​𝑑t=∫0TSt​d​QtQT.\\displaystyle\\text{VWAP}_{T}:=\\frac{\\int_{0}^{T}S_{t}V_{t}dt}{\\int_{0}^{T}V_{t}dt}=\\frac{\\int_{0}^{T}S_{t}dQ_{t}}{Q_{T}}.\n(2.2)\nRemark 2.2.\nThe above definition of the VWAP can also be formulated as:\nVWAPT=∫0TSt​d​xt,\\text{VWAP}_{T}=\\int_{0}^{T}S_{t}dx_{t},\nwhere xt:=QtQTx_{t}:=\\frac{Q_{t}}{Q_{T}}. This formulation is often used in the literature but it has an important drawback as the above integral is not 𝔽\\mathbb{F}-adapted. Its natural filtration is indeed (𝒢t)t(\\mathcal{G}_{t})_{t} where:\n𝒢t:=ℱt∨σ⁡(QT).\\mathcal{G}_{t}:=\\mathcal{F}_{t}\\vee\\sigma(Q_{T}).\nRemark 2.3.\nIn the above definition of V​W​A​PTVWAP_{T}, we did not include our own volume. An alternative definition, including our trades, is\nVWAPT′:=∫0TSt​(Vt+vt)​𝑑tQT+q0.\\text{VWAP}^{\\prime}_{T}:=\\frac{\\int_{0}^{T}S_{t}(V_{t}+v_{t})dt}{Q_{T}+q_{0}}.\nWe shall see in the appendix of this article that the results we obtain with our simpler definition can be easily modified to be true in the case of the alternative definition.\nThe rationale for our optimization criterion (2.1) is the following. We consider a stock trader or an asset manager who wants to sell q0q_{0} shares at the VWAP over the period [0,T][0,T]. For that purpose, he signs with an intermediary (typically a broker) a guaranteed VWAP contract.1111\n 11\n This is not an agency VWAP since, here, the VWAP is guaranteed (although its value is not known ex ante). He gives the intermediary its q0q_{0} shares at time 0 and he receives at time TT, q0q_{0} times the VWAP computed over the period [0,T][0,T], minus a premium – hereafter denoted π⁡(q0)\\pi(q_{0}) – to compensate the intermediary for the service and the associated costs, this premium being agreed upon at time 00. The problem we address is the problem of the intermediary: he receives q0q_{0} shares and sells them over the period [0,T][0,T] to obtain XTX_{T} on its cash account at time TT. Then, he gives his client q0​VWAPT−π⁡(q0)q_{0}\\text{VWAP}_{T}-\\pi(q_{0}) in cash. Therefore, if the intermediary has a constant absolute risk aversion γ\\gamma, his liquidation strategy is obtained by maximizing\n𝔼⁡[−exp⁡(−γ⁡(XT−q0​VWAPT+π⁡(q0)))]=exp⁡(−γ​π​(q0))​𝔼​[−exp⁡(−γ⁡(XT−q0​VWAPT))].\\mathbb{E}\\left[-\\exp\\left(-\\gamma(X_{T}-q_{0}\\text{VWAP}_{T}+\\pi(q_{0}))\\right)\\right]=\\exp(-\\gamma\\pi(q_{0}))\\mathbb{E}\\left[-\\exp\\left(-\\gamma(X_{T}-q_{0}\\text{VWAP}_{T})\\right)\\right].\nSince π⁡(q0)\\pi(q_{0}) is agreed upon at time 00, the objective function is simply:\n𝔼⁡[−exp⁡(−γ⁡(XT−q0​VWAPT))].\\mathbb{E}\\left[-\\exp\\left(-\\gamma(X_{T}-q_{0}\\text{VWAP}_{T})\\right)\\right].\nNow, to decide upon the value π⁡(q0)\\pi(q_{0}), we shall compute the reservation price of the intermediary, that is the price at which the intermediary is indifferent between accepting the contract and refusing it. This approach for pricing, also called indifference pricing, leads to the following definition for the premium of a guaranteed VWAP:1212\n 12\n The premium in percentage is then π⁡(q0)q0​S0\\frac{\\pi(q_{0})}{q_{0}S_{0}}. However, this is expressed in percentage of the initial price. In practice, some guaranteed VWAP contracts are also priced in basis points of the realized VWAP. We refer to Appendix B for this different definition of the premium and its consequences on our approach. Numerically, the two approaches provide similar figures in basis point of their respective reference price.\nπ(q0)=1γlog(−supv∈𝒜𝔼[−exp(−γ(XT−q0VWAPT))]).\\pi(q_{0})=\\frac{1}{\\gamma}\\log\\left(-\\sup_{v\\in\\mathcal{A}}\\mathbb{E}\\left[-\\exp\\left(-\\gamma(X_{T}-q_{0}\\text{VWAP}_{T})\\right)\\right]\\right).\nOur goal in this paper is twofold: (i) we want to solve the optimization problem, that is to find an optimal liquidation strategy vv, and (ii) we want to find the value of π⁡(q0)\\pi(q_{0}).\n2.2 First properties\nWe derive here the key formulas for XTX_{T} and VWAPT\\text{VWAP}_{T}:\nLemma 2.1.\nFor any v∈𝒜v\\in\\mathcal{A}, we obtain:\nXT=q0​S0−∫0q0F⁡(z)​𝑑z−∫0TVt​L​(vtVt)​𝑑t+∫0Tqt​σ​d​Wt.X_{T}=q_{0}S_{0}-\\int_{0}^{q_{0}}F(z)dz-\\int_{0}^{T}V_{t}L\\left(\\frac{v_{t}}{V_{t}}\\right)dt+\\int_{0}^{T}q_{t}\\sigma have:\nVWAPT=S0+∫0T(1−QtQT)​σ​d​Wt−∫0TVtQT​F​(q0−qt)​𝑑t.\\text{VWAP}_{T}=S_{0}+\\int_{0}^{T}\\left(1-\\frac{Q_{t}}{Q_{T}}\\right)\\sigma It states that, in the absence of permanent market impact, the optimal strategy is to have a trading curve that has the same shape as the relative market volume curve. One consequence is that, in practice, as far as the trading strategy is concerned, when permanent market impact can be (or is) ignored, one is interested in the estimation of the relative market volume curve and not in the estimation of the absolute value of the market volume. This remark is particularly important to understand why the deterministic market volume assumption provides a rather acceptable approximation of the real case for VWAP trading. Although the total volume traded over a day is highly variable, we know that the relative market volume curve is stable from one day to the other (except on witching days). Since the cumulated volume QTQ_{T} only appears in the execution strategy through the ratio QtQT\\frac{Q_{t}}{Q_{T}}, considering it stochastic does not play any role if we have already assumed that the relative market volume curve is deterministic.1313\n 13\n In practice, most institutions use relative market volume curves computed in advance, based on historical data. The value of QTQ_{T} is however important to determine the premium of the guaranteed VWAP contract. Since this premium must be decided upon at time t=0t=0, the value of QTQ_{T} must be understood1414\n 14\n We ignore here part of the risk. as a forecast at time 00 of the total market volume over the period [0,T][0,T].\nThe above remarks only apply in the absence of permanent market impact but the assumption of a deterministic market volume is acceptable if we deviate slightly through the introduction of a small permanent market impact. result permits to understand the role played by permanent market impact. The rationale underlying this point is that the intermediary is going to pay q0​VWAPTq_{0}\\text{VWAP}_{T} to the client and therefore he has an incentive to sell rapidly so that the price moves down, resulting in a lower VWAP.
